docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
This document explains the core algorithms used in the A-Maze-ing project.

The project mainly relies on: - Depth-First Search (DFS) for maze generation - Breadth-First Search (BFS) for maze solving

These algorithms are responsible for: - creating valid mazes - generating paths - solving the maze - visualizing exploration and traversal

docs.title: 📁 Main Files
docs.text:
mazegen/
├── generator.py
└── solver.py

docs.title: 🧠 Overview
docs.text:
The project uses two different graph traversal algorithms:

Algorithm Purpose DFS Maze generation BFS Shortest path solving

Both algorithms operate on the maze's expanded grid representation.

docs.title: 🌱 DFS Maze Generation
docs.text:
Main function:

def dfs_generator(maze: Maze) -> None:

Main file:

mazegen/generator.py

docs.title: 🧩 Goal of DFS
docs.text:
DFS is used to: - carve paths through walls - visit every logical cell - create a valid maze structure - generate a perfect maze

A perfect maze means: - every cell is reachable - there is only one valid path between cells - no loops exist

docs.title: 🧠 Expanded Grid System
docs.text:
The maze internally uses an expanded grid.

Logical cells are separated by walls.

Example:

# # # # #
# . # . #
# # # # #
# . # . #
# # # # #

Logical coordinates are converted using:

(y * 2 + 1), (x * 2 + 1)

This allows the algorithm to: - carve walls - connect cells - preserve maze structure

docs.title: 🔄 DFS Traversal Logic
docs.text:
The DFS algorithm:

  1. Starts at the first logical cell
  2. Marks the current cell as visited
  3. Randomly selects a direction
  4. Moves two cells away
  5. Breaks the wall between cells
  6. Recursively continues traversal

docs.title: 🎲 Randomized Directions
docs.text:
The directions are shuffled using:

random.sample(directions, len(directions))

This guarantees: - randomized mazes - different layouts every execution - procedural generation behavior

docs.title: 🪓 Wall Breaking
docs.text:
When DFS moves to a new cell:

Current Cell -> Wall -> Next Cell

the wall between both cells is removed.

This creates: - corridors - connected paths - valid maze routes

docs.title: 📌 DFS Characteristics
docs.text: Property Behavior Traversal Type Recursive Path Type Deep exploration Maze Style Long corridors Randomness High Guarantees Fully connected maze

docs.title: 🚪 Entry and Exit Integration
docs.text:
After DFS generation:

apply_entry_exit(maze)

opens: - the entry cell - the exit cell - external maze doors

The project validates that: - entry and exit are located on maze borders - coordinates are valid - doors connect correctly with the expanded grid

docs.title: 🛡️ Maze Validation
docs.text:
The generation system validates: - invalid open spaces - malformed structures - impossible layouts

Main validation:

check_open_areas()

This prevents: - large empty spaces - invalid 3x3 open blocks

docs.title: 🧱 Imperfect Maze Generation
docs.text:
If the maze is configured as:

PERFECT=False

the algorithm uses:

break_walls()

to: - remove extra walls - create loops - generate multiple possible paths

This transforms the perfect DFS maze into an imperfect maze.

docs.title: 🔎 BFS Maze Solving
docs.text:
Main function:

def bfs_solve_maze(maze: Maze)

Main file:

mazegen/solver.py

docs.title: 🎯 Goal of BFS
docs.text: BFS is used to: - find the shortest path - solve the maze - reconstruct the optimal route - generate exploration animations

docs.title: 📦 BFS Data Structures
docs.text:
The solver uses:

Structure Purpose Queue (deque) Exploration order Set (visited) Prevent revisits Dictionary (parent) Path reconstruction List (explored) Animation visualization

docs.title: 🌊 BFS Traversal Logic
docs.text:
The BFS algorithm:

  1. Starts at the entry point
  2. Explores neighboring cells
  3. Expands layer by layer
  4. Continues until the exit is found
  5. Reconstructs the shortest path

Unlike DFS: - BFS explores breadth-first - guarantees the shortest path

docs.title: 🧭 Valid Movement Rules
docs.text:
The solver ignores: - walls (1) - logo cells (2) - already visited cells - out-of-bounds positions

This ensures: - safe traversal - valid pathfinding - no infinite loops

docs.title: 🧩 Path Reconstruction
docs.text:
Once the exit is found:

parent[(new_y, new_x)] = (y, x)

stores: - where each cell came from

The algorithm then reconstructs the path: - backwards from exit - until the entry point is reached

Finally: - the path is reversed - producing the final solution order

docs.title: 🎞️ Explored Cells Animation
docs.text:
BFS also stores:

explored.append((new_y, new_x))

This allows the renderer to: - visualize exploration - animate the solver - display visited cells progressively

docs.title: 📌 BFS Characteristics
docs.text: Property Behavior Traversal Type Iterative Exploration Style Layer-by-layer Path Guarantee Shortest path Memory Usage Higher than DFS Animation Friendly Yes

docs.title: ⚖️ DFS vs BFS
docs.text: DFS BFS Generates mazes Solves mazes Recursive Iterative Deep traversal Breadth traversal Randomized Deterministic Creates paths Finds shortest path

docs.title: 🎯 Algorithm Goals
docs.text:
The algorithm system was designed to: - generate valid procedural mazes - guarantee solvable layouts - provide visual algorithm demonstrations - support animation systems - separate generation and solving logic cleanly

The combination of DFS and BFS creates: - randomized maze structures - reliable shortest-path solving - interactive visualization systems - reproducible procedural generation

docs.title: Export System
docs.text:
This document explains the export and utility systems used in the A-Maze-ing project.

The export system is responsible for: - Converting maze data into hexadecimal values - Exporting maze information into a .txt file - Converting paths into N, E, S, W directions - Handling logical maze cell serialization

docs.title: 📁 Main Files
docs.text:
utils/
├── export_utils.py
├── hex_utils.py
└── path_utils.py

docs.title: 🧠 Overview
docs.text:
The export system converts the generated maze into a structured output format.

The exported file contains: - Hexadecimal maze representation - Entry coordinates - Exit coordinates - BFS solution path directions

This output format follows the project requirements and allows the maze data to be reconstructed later.

docs.title: 📦 Export Pipeline
docs.text:
Generated Maze
      │
      ▼
maze_to_hex()
      │
      ▼
path_to_directions()
      │
      ▼
export_maze()
      │
      ▼
output_maze.txt

docs.title: 📝 Main Export Function
docs.text:
Main file:

utils/export_utils.py

Main function:

def export_maze(
    maze: Maze,
    path: list[tuple[int, int]],
    output_file: str
) -> None:

This function: - converts the maze into hexadecimal values - extracts entry and exit coordinates - converts the BFS path into directions - writes all information into the output file

docs.title: 📄 Exported File Structure
docs.text: The generated output file contains:

docs.title: 1. Hexadecimal Maze Representation
docs.text:
Each logical maze cell is converted into a hexadecimal value.

Example:

F F F F
9 2 A 6
D 4 1 3

Each hexadecimal value represents which walls are closed around the cell.

docs.title: 2. Entry Coordinates
docs.text:
Example:

0,0

docs.title: 3. Exit Coordinates
docs.text:
Example:

19,19

docs.title: 4. Path Directions
docs.text:
Example:

EESSWWNN

The directions represent the shortest BFS path from entry to exit.

docs.title: 🔢 Hexadecimal Conversion
docs.text:
Main file:

utils/hex_utils.py

Main function:

def maze_to_hex(maze: Maze) -> list[list[str]]:

docs.title: 🧠 How the Hex System Works
docs.text:
Each logical maze cell checks its surrounding walls:

Direction Bit Value North 1 East 2 South 4 West 8

The values are summed and converted into hexadecimal.

docs.title: 📌 Example
docs.text:
If a cell has: - North wall - West wall

then:

1 + 8 = 9

Hex value:

9

docs.title: 🧩 Expanded Grid Conversion
docs.text:
The maze internally uses an expanded grid system.

Logical coordinates are converted into grid coordinates:

(y * 2 + 1), (x * 2 + 1)

This allows: - walls - paths - openings

to exist between logical cells.

docs.title: 🧭 Path Direction Conversion
docs.text:
Main file:

utils/path_utils.py

Main function:

def path_to_directions(
    path: list[tuple[int, int]]
) -> list[str]:

This function converts BFS coordinates into: - N - E - S - W

directions.

docs.title: 📌 Example
docs.text:
Coordinate path:

[(1,1), (1,2), (2,2)]

becomes:

["E", "S"]

docs.title: 🖨️ File Printing Utility
docs.text:
The export system also contains a helper function:

def print_maze_file(output_file: str) -> None:

This function: - opens the exported file - reads its contents - prints the result to the terminal

It is mainly used for: - debugging - testing - output verification

docs.title: 🚨 Error Handling
docs.text:
The export system handles: - missing files - permission errors - invalid output access

using try/except blocks.

Example:

print_maze_file() failed -> File not found

docs.title: 🎯 Goals of the Export System
docs.text:
The export system was designed to: - serialize maze data - match project output requirements - simplify debugging - convert internal structures into readable formats - provide reusable utility functions

It acts as the final conversion layer between: - maze generation - pathfinding - file output - external representation

docs.title: Maze Generator
docs.text:
This document explains the reusable maze generation module used in the A-Maze-ing project.

The maze generator is the core system responsible for: - creating the maze structure - applying entry and exit points - validating maze rules - solving the maze - exporting the final result - providing a reusable package through .whl

docs.title: 📁 Main Files
docs.text:
mazegen/
├── __init__.py
├── Maze.py
├── MazeGenerator.py
├── generator.py
└── solver.py

docs.title: 🧱 Maze Class
docs.text:
Main file:

mazegen/Maze.py

The Maze class stores the basic maze data.

class Maze:

It contains: - maze width - maze height - entry coordinates - exit coordinates - expanded grid - expanded grid width - expanded grid height

docs.title: 🧩 Expanded Grid
docs.text:
The project uses an expanded grid representation.

For a maze with logical size:

WIDTH x HEIGHT

the internal grid size becomes:

(2 * WIDTH + 1) x (2 * HEIGHT + 1)

This allows the maze to store: - logical cells - walls between cells - external borders - opened doors

Example:

logical cell -> expanded position

(x, y) -> (x * 2 + 1, y * 2 + 1)

docs.title: 🏗️ MazeGenerator Class
docs.text:
Main file:

mazegen/MazeGenerator.py

The MazeGenerator class controls the full maze generation pipeline.

class MazeGenerator:

It receives:

width: int
height: int
entry: tuple[int, int]
exit: tuple[int, int]
perfect: bool
seed: int | None

docs.title: ⚙️ Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
The main method is:

def generate_maze(self) -> Maze:

This method coordinates the helper functions from generator.py and solver.py.

Pipeline:

MazeGenerator.generate_maze()
        │
        ▼
Create Maze object
        │
        ▼
dfs_generator()
        │
        ▼
apply_entry_exit()
        │
        ▼
check_open_areas()
        │
        ▼
add_42_logo()
        │
        ▼
break_walls() if PERFECT=False
        │
        ▼
bfs_solve_maze()
        │
        ▼
Return valid Maze

docs.title: 🌱 DFS Integration
docs.text:
The generator calls:

dfs_generator(maze)

from:

mazegen/generator.py

This function: - carves the maze paths - visits reachable cells - creates the base perfect maze structure

The DFS details are documented in:

algorithms.md

docs.title: 🚪 Entry and Exit
docs.text:
The generator calls:

apply_entry_exit(maze)

This function: - converts logical entry and exit coordinates into expanded grid coordinates - opens the internal entry and exit cells - validates that entry and exit are placed on maze borders - opens the external door for each one

docs.title: 🛡️ Maze Validation
docs.text:
The generator calls:

check_open_areas(maze)

This function prevents invalid open spaces by rejecting mazes containing a fully open 3x3 area.

If the generated maze does not pass validation, the generator tries again.

docs.title: 4️⃣ 42 Logo Integration
docs.text:
The generator calls:

add_42_logo(maze)

This function adds the visible 42 pattern to the maze.

The logo is represented inside the expanded grid using closed cells.

If the maze is too small for the logo, the function returns an empty list and the program prints a warning message.

docs.title: 🧱 Perfect and Imperfect Mazes
docs.text: The project supports two maze types through the PERFECT configuration value.

docs.title: PERFECT=True
docs.text:
The maze keeps the original DFS-generated structure.

This means: - the maze is fully connected - the maze has a single main route structure - no extra walls are removed after generation

docs.title: PERFECT=False
docs.text:
The generator calls:

break_walls(maze, logo_pos)

This function: - removes additional walls - creates extra routes - makes the maze imperfect - protects the 42 logo cells from being overwritten

docs.title: 🔎 BFS Integration
docs.text:
After generation, the maze is solved using:

bfs_solve_maze(maze)

from:

mazegen/solver.py

This confirms that: - the maze is solvable - a valid path exists between entry and exit

If BFS cannot find a path, the generation attempt is rejected and the generator tries again.

docs.title: 🧭 Solver Method
docs.text:
The class also provides:

def solve(self, algorithm: str) -> tuple[list[tuple[int, int]], list[tuple[int, int]]]:

Currently supported algorithm:

bfs

The method returns: - the final shortest path - explored cells used for pathfinding animation

Example:

path, explored = generator.solve("bfs")

docs.title: 📤 Export Method
docs.text:
The class provides:

def export(self, output_file: str) -> None:

This method calls the export system:

export_maze(self.maze, self.path, output_file)

The export logic is documented in:

export-system.md

docs.title: 📦 Reusable Package
docs.text:
The mazegen directory is designed to work as a reusable Python package.

This allows the maze generation logic to be used outside the main graphical application.

The reusable package contains: - Maze - MazeGenerator - DFS generation helpers - BFS solving helpers

The MLX rendering, menu system, assets, and gameplay logic are not part of the reusable package.

docs.title: 📄 Package Public API
docs.text:
The package exposes its main classes through:

mazegen/__init__.py

Example:

from .MazeGenerator import MazeGenerator
from .Maze import Maze

__all__ = [
    "MazeGenerator",
    "Maze"
]

This allows external projects to import:

from mazegen import MazeGenerator

docs.title: 🛠️ Building the .whl
docs.text:
The package can be built using Python build tools.

Install build:

pip install build

Build the package:

python -m build

This creates:

dist/
├── mazegen-1.0.0.tar.gz
└── mazegen-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: 📥 Installing the Package
docs.text:
The generated wheel can be installed with:

pip install dist/mazegen-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

or force reinstalled with:

pip install --force-reinstall dist/mazegen-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: 🧪 Example Usage
docs.text:
After installing the wheel:

from mazegen import MazeGenerator

generator = MazeGenerator(
    width=20,
    height=20,
    entry=(0, 0),
    exit=(19, 19),
    perfect=True,
    seed=42
)

maze = generator.generate_maze()
path, explored = generator.solve("bfs")

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose of the Maze Generator Module
docs.text:
The maze generator module was designed to: - keep the maze logic separate from rendering - make the project easier to maintain - support reuse in future projects - provide a clean API - satisfy the reusable module requirement - allow package distribution through .whl

This separation makes the project more modular by keeping the core maze engine independent from the visual MLX application.

docs.title: MLX Library
docs.text:
This document explains how the MiniLibX (MLX) library is used in the A-Maze-ing project.

MiniLibX is a small graphical library commonly used in 42 School projects. It provides basic tools to: - open a window - load images - draw images to the screen - handle keyboard input - listen to window events - run a graphical loop

In this project, MLX is used to display the maze, menus, themes, player movement, BFS animations, and visual feedback.

docs.title: 📁 Main Files
docs.text:
render/
├── mlx_renderer.py
├── draw_maze.py
├── menu.py
├── Assets.py
├── converter.py
└── GameState.py

docs.title: 🧠 What MLX Does
docs.text:
MLX works as the graphical layer of the project.

It does not generate the maze and it does not solve the maze.

Instead, it receives data from the project and displays it visually.

Maze generation
      │
      ▼
Maze grid / path / state
      │
      ▼
MLX renderer
      │
      ▼
Window display

docs.title: 🪟 Creating a Window
docs.text:
The first step in any MLX program is initializing MLX and creating a window.

In this project, this happens inside:

def mlx_window(game: GameState) -> None:

Example from the project:

mlx = Mlx()
mlx_ptr = mlx.mlx_init()

win_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_window(
    mlx_ptr,
    WINDOW_WIDTH,
    WINDOW_HEIGHT,
    "A-MAZE-ING"
)

This creates the main game window.

The project uses:

WINDOW_WIDTH = 1600
WINDOW_HEIGHT = 900

docs.title: 🖼️ Images in MLX
docs.text:
MiniLibX works best with .xpm images.

Because of that, the project converts image assets into XPM before loading them.

Examples of loaded assets: - walls - floors - trails - ducks - exit doors - banners - menu backgrounds

docs.title: 📦 Asset Loading
docs.text:
The Assets class loads and stores the images used by the renderer.

Main file:

render/Assets.py

Example:

self.wall, _, _ = mlx.mlx_xpm_file_to_image(
    mlx_ptr,
    f"assets/generated/{wall_file}_{tile_size}.xpm"
)

This loads an XPM image and stores it so it can be drawn later.

docs.title: 🔄 PNG / JPEG to XPM Conversion
docs.text:
The project stores original assets as PNG or JPEG files.

Before MLX can use them, they are: 1. resized 2. converted to XPM 3. saved in assets/generated/

Main file:

render/converter.py

Main functions:

generate_scaled_asset()
convert_to_xpm()
generate_all_assets()

Example:

os.system(f"magick {png_path} {xpm_path}")

The project uses ImageMagick through the magick command to perform the conversion.

docs.title: 📐 Dynamic Asset Scaling
docs.text:
The maze can have different sizes, so the tile size is calculated dynamically.

This prevents the maze from being too large for the screen.

Example:

def calculate_tile_size(game: GameState) -> int:

The tile size depends on: - maze width - maze height - available window width - available window height - banner space

Once the tile size is known, assets are generated for that exact size.

docs.title: 🧱 Drawing Images to the Window
docs.text:
MLX draws images using:

mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window()

Example from the project:

mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(
    mlx_ptr,
    win_ptr,
    base_tile,
    screen_x,
    screen_y
)

This places an image at a specific pixel position.

docs.title: 🧩 Tile-Based Rendering
docs.text:
The maze is drawn tile by tile.

Each value in the maze grid represents a different visual element:

0 = floor
1 = wall
2 = 42 wall
3 = duck/player
4 = trail/path

The renderer reads the grid and chooses which image to draw.

Example logic:

if cell == 3:
    base_tile = assets.floor
elif cell == 0:
    base_tile = assets.floor
elif cell == 1:
    base_tile = assets.wall
elif cell == 2:
    base_tile = assets.wall_42
else:
    base_tile = assets.trail

docs.title: 🦆 Drawing the Player
docs.text:
The duck is drawn as a separate image on top of the floor.

This is important because the player should not permanently modify the maze grid.

Example:

if cell == 3:
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(
        mlx_ptr,
        win_ptr,
        assets.duck,
        screen_x,
        screen_y
    )

This allows the player to move without destroying walls, floors, or trails.

docs.title: 🚪 Drawing Entry and Exit
docs.text:
The maze entry and exit are logical cells.

For rendering, they are converted to expanded grid positions.

The renderer uses:

logical_to_grid()
calculate_door_position()

These functions are used to draw the entry and exit doors in the correct position.

docs.title: 🧭 Coordinate Systems
docs.text: The project uses two coordinate systems:

docs.title: Logical Coordinates
docs.text:
Used by the configuration file and maze structure.

Example:

ENTRY=0,0
EXIT=19,19

docs.title: Grid Coordinates
docs.text:
Used by the expanded internal maze grid.

Conversion:

grid_x = logical_x * 2 + 1
grid_y = logical_y * 2 + 1

This allows the renderer to draw: - cells - walls - corridors - doors

correctly.

docs.title: 🎮 Keyboard Input
docs.text:
MLX can react to keyboard input using hooks.

In this project, keyboard input is handled with:

mlx.mlx_key_hook()

Example:

mlx.mlx_key_hook(
    win_ptr,
    lambda key, param: key_hook(
        key,
        game,
        frame,
        param,
        mlx,
        mlx_ptr,
        win_ptr
    ),
    None
)

The key_hook() function controls: - menu selection - maze regeneration - BFS animation - player mode - theme switching - exiting the game

docs.title: ⌨️ Key Controls
docs.text:
The project uses numeric keys and arrow keys.

1        Generate new maze
2        Show shortest path
3        Show BFS exploration animation
4        Player mode
5        Change theme
6 / ESC  Exit
Arrows   Move player

docs.title: 🎮 Game State and MLX
docs.text:
MLX itself does not know what mode the game is in.

The project stores that information inside:

class GameState:

The renderer checks the game state every frame.

Example states:

game.mode
game.theme
game.show_path
game.animate_bfs
game.playing
game.game_won

This allows MLX to draw different things depending on the current mode.

docs.title: 🔁 The MLX Loop
docs.text:
MLX uses a loop to keep the window alive.

In this project:

mlx.mlx_loop_hook(
    mlx_ptr,
    on_loop,
    None
)

mlx.mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)

The loop repeatedly calls on_loop().

This function updates: - menu rendering - maze rendering - animations - player movement display - exit animation

docs.title: 🎞️ Animation With MLX
docs.text:
MLX does not provide a complex animation system by itself.

Instead, the project creates animation manually using: - frame counters - time checks - partial path drawing - repeated redraws

Example:

frame = [0]
last_time = [time.time()]

The renderer only advances the animation when enough time has passed.

Example:

if now - last_time[0] >= 0.05:

This prevents animations from running too fast.

docs.title: 🦆 Path Animation
docs.text:
Option 2 shows the shortest path.

The renderer progressively draws part of the path:

game.path[:frame[0]]

This creates the effect of the duck moving through the maze.

docs.title: 🌊 BFS Exploration Animation
docs.text:
Option 3 shows how BFS explores the maze.

Instead of displaying only the final path, it displays explored cells:

game.explored[:frame[0]]

This visualizes the search process step by step.

docs.title: 🚪 Exit Animation
docs.text:
The exit uses two images:

assets.exit
assets.exit2

The renderer alternates between them using time:

animation_frame = int(time.time() * 3.33) % 2

This creates a simple animated portal effect.

docs.title: 🧹 Clearing and Syncing the Window
docs.text:
Sometimes the renderer needs to clear the old screen before drawing a new state.

Example:

mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)

The project also uses:

mlx.mlx_do_sync(mlx_ptr)

to help synchronize visual updates.

This is useful when: - changing themes - regenerating the maze - switching modes - entering player mode

docs.title: ❌ Closing the Window
docs.text:
The project handles the window close event with:

mlx.mlx_hook(
    win_ptr,
    33,
    0,
    close,
    None
)

The close() function exits the program:

def close(param: Any) -> None:
    os._exit(0)

The user can also quit with:

ESC
6

docs.title: 🎨 Themes With MLX
docs.text:
The renderer supports different visual themes.

Current themes:

normal
gothic

The selected theme changes which assets are loaded.

Example:

f"assets/generated/{theme}_floor_{tile_size}.xpm"

This allows the same maze logic to be displayed with different visual styles.

docs.title: 🧱 MLX Limitations
docs.text:
MLX is intentionally simple.

It does not provide: - advanced UI widgets - built-in animation tools - sprite management - automatic scaling - layout systems - scene management

Because of that, the project manually handles: - asset conversion - image scaling - menu drawing - animation timing - player movement - screen updates

docs.title: 🧠 Why MLX Was Used
docs.text:
MLX was used because: - it is part of the 42 graphics ecosystem - it teaches low-level rendering concepts - it gives direct control over pixels and images - it integrates well with simple game loops - it is suitable for tile-based projects

For this project, MLX is enough to create: - a graphical maze - menus - animations - player movement - theme switching

docs.title: 🏗️ Role of MLX in A-Maze-ing
docs.text:
MLX acts as the visual interface between the user and the maze engine.

MazeGenerator
      │
      ▼
Maze + Path + Explored Cells
      │
      ▼
GameState
      │
      ▼
MLX Renderer
      │
      ▼
Window Output

The maze generation system stays independent from MLX.

This separation keeps the project modular: - mazegen/ handles maze logic - render/ handles graphics and interaction

docs.title: 🎯 Summary
docs.text:
In A-Maze-ing, MiniLibX is used to: - open the game window - load XPM images - draw the maze - render menus and banners - handle keyboard input - animate BFS and pathfinding - display player movement - support visual themes

The project builds a higher-level rendering system on top of MLX by combining: - GameState - dynamic assets - tile rendering - event hooks - animation logic

This allows a simple graphics library to support a complete interactive maze visualizer.

docs.title: Parsing System
docs.text:
This document explains the configuration parsing system used in the A-Maze-ing project.

The parser is responsible for: - Reading maze configuration files - Validating required parameters - Converting values to proper Python types - Detecting invalid or duplicated data - Ensuring the maze configuration is valid before generation

docs.title: 📁 Main File
docs.text:
parsing/
└── config_parser.py

docs.title: 🧠 Overview
docs.text:
The parser uses a simple KEY=VALUE configuration format.

Example:

WIDTH=20
HEIGHT=20
ENTRY=0,0
EXIT=19,19
OUTPUT_FILE=output_maze.txt
PERFECT=True
SEED=42

The configuration is: - read from a .txt file - converted into a Python dictionary - validated - transformed into usable Python types

docs.title: ⚙️ Main Responsibilities
docs.text:
The parsing system performs several validation and transformation steps:

  • File loading
  • Syntax validation
  • Required key validation
  • Duplicate key detection
  • Type conversion
  • Semantic validation

docs.title: 📥 Configuration File Path
docs.text:
The parser first checks if a configuration file was provided through command-line arguments.

def get_config_path() -> str:

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• If a .txt file path is provided:
  • it is used as the configuration source
  • If no argument is provided:
  • an exception is raised

docs.title: 🔑 Mandatory Keys Validation
docs.text:
The parser validates that all required configuration keys exist.

Required keys:

WIDTH
HEIGHT
ENTRY
EXIT
OUTPUT_FILE
PERFECT

If one or more keys are missing:

ConfigError:
Missing required key(s)

is raised.

docs.title: 📝 Configuration Parsing
docs.text:
The main parsing function is:

def parse_config(file_path: str) -> dict[str, Any]:

This function: - opens the configuration file - reads it line by line - validates syntax - stores values in a dictionary

docs.title: Empty Lines
docs.text:
Empty lines are ignored.

Example:

WIDTH=20

HEIGHT=20

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Lines starting with # are ignored.

Example:

# Maze configuration
WIDTH=20

docs.title: Duplicate Key Detection
docs.text:
If the same key appears twice:

WIDTH=20
WIDTH=30

the parser raises:

Duplicate key 'WIDTH'

docs.title: Invalid Format Detection
docs.text:
If a line does not contain =:

WIDTH 20

the parser raises:

Invalid format on line X

docs.title: 🔄 Type Conversion System
docs.text:
After parsing the raw strings, the values are converted into proper Python types.

Main conversion function:

def convert_config(config: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:

docs.title: 🔢 Integer Conversion
docs.text:
The following keys are converted to integers:

WIDTH
HEIGHT
SEED

Example:

WIDTH=20

becomes:

20

docs.title: 📍 Coordinate Conversion
docs.text:
The following keys are converted into tuples:

ENTRY
EXIT

Example:

ENTRY=0,0

becomes:

(0, 0)

docs.title: ✅ Boolean Conversion
docs.text:
The PERFECT key is converted into a boolean value.

Example:

PERFECT=True

becomes:

True

Supported values:

True
False

Invalid values raise:

PERFECT must be True or False

docs.title: 🛡️ Semantic Validation
docs.text: The parser also validates logical maze constraints.

docs.title: Positive Dimensions
docs.text:
Maze dimensions must be positive.

Invalid example:

WIDTH=-5

docs.title: Entry and Exit Validation
docs.text:
The parser ensures: - entry and exit are different - coordinates are inside maze bounds

Invalid example:

ENTRY=50,50

for a small maze raises an exception.

docs.title: 🚨 Error Handling
docs.text:
The parsing system uses a custom exception:

class ConfigError(Exception):

This provides: - cleaner error reporting - easier debugging - centralized configuration validation errors

docs.title: 🧩 Parsing Pipeline
docs.text:
config.txt
     │
     ▼
parse_config()
     │
     ▼
Dictionary Creation
     │
     ▼
Mandatory Key Validation
     │
     ▼
convert_config()
     │
     ▼
Type Conversion
     │
     ▼
Semantic Validation
     │
     ▼
Validated Configuration

docs.title: 📦 Final Output Example
docs.text:
After parsing and conversion:

{
    "WIDTH": 20,
    "HEIGHT": 20,
    "ENTRY": (0, 0),
    "EXIT": (19, 19),
    "OUTPUT_FILE": "output_maze.txt",
    "PERFECT": True,
    "SEED": 42
}

docs.title: 🎯 Goals of the Parsing System
docs.text:
The parsing system was designed to: - simplify maze configuration - provide strong validation - prevent invalid maze generation - improve debugging - keep the project modular and maintainable

It acts as the first validation layer before any maze generation or rendering begins.

docs.title: Render System
docs.text:
This document explains the rendering systems used in the A-Maze-ing project.

The render system is responsible for: - graphical visualization using MiniLibX - menu and banner rendering - asset loading and scaling - player visualization - animation systems - real-time game updates

docs.title: 📁 Main Files
docs.text:
render/
├── Assets.py
├── converter.py
├── draw_maze.py
├── GameState.py
├── menu.py
└── mlx_renderer.py

docs.title: 🧠 Overview
docs.text:
The rendering system combines: - MiniLibX graphical rendering - dynamic asset loading - tile-based visualization - gameplay systems - real-time animations - menu and UI rendering

The renderer is responsible for: - drawing the maze - displaying gameplay elements - animating BFS/path systems - handling themes - rendering player movement - updating the graphical interface in real time

docs.title: 🖼️ MLX Rendering System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/mlx_renderer.py

Main function:

def mlx_window(game: GameState) -> None:

This function: - initializes MLX - creates the game window - loads graphical assets - handles events - updates the rendering loop

docs.title: 🪟 Window System
docs.text:
The game window uses:

WINDOW_WIDTH = 1600
WINDOW_HEIGHT = 900

The renderer dynamically scales the maze to fit inside the window.

The bottom section of the screen is reserved for the banner UI.

docs.title: 🎮 Game Modes
docs.text:
The renderer supports multiple game states.

Main states:

Mode Description MENU Theme selection screen GAME Main gameplay screen

Gameplay options:

Key Action 1 Generate new maze 2 Show BFS solution path 3 Show BFS exploration animation 4 Player mode 5 Change theme ESC / 6 Exit game

docs.title: 🧩 GameState System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/GameState.py

The GameState class stores all runtime game information.

class GameState:

It stores: - current mode - selected theme - animation states - player position - current maze - BFS path - explored nodes - gameplay flags

docs.title: 🧠 Main Stored Data
docs.text:
Examples:

self.mode
self.theme
self.playing
self.show_path
self.animate_bfs
self.player_x
self.player_y
self.path
self.explored

The class acts as a centralized runtime state manager.

docs.title: 🎨 Asset System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/Assets.py

The Assets class loads all XPM images used by the game.

class Assets:

Loaded assets include: - walls - floors - trails - ducks - exit doors - animated exits - banners

docs.title: 🖼️ Theme System
docs.text:
The renderer supports multiple themes.

Current themes:

normal
gothic

The selected theme changes: - walls - floors - ducks - trails - exits

The assets are loaded dynamically depending on: - theme - tile size

docs.title: 🔄 Asset Conversion System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/converter.py

The project stores original assets as: - PNG - JPEG

They are dynamically converted into: - XPM

because MiniLibX requires the XPM format.

docs.title: 📦 Asset Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
The conversion system:

  1. loads the original image
  2. resizes the image
  3. converts the image into XPM
  4. stores the generated file

Main functions:

generate_scaled_asset()
convert_to_xpm()
generate_all_assets()

docs.title: 📐 Dynamic Tile Scaling
docs.text:
The renderer dynamically calculates tile size:

def calculate_tile_size(game: GameState) -> int:

This allows: - small mazes - large mazes - fullscreen scaling

without manually resizing assets.

docs.title: 🧱 Maze Drawing System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/draw_maze.py

Main function:

def draw_maze(...)

This function: - renders the maze grid - draws walls and floors - draws the player - draws BFS trails - renders the animated exit - centers the maze on screen

docs.title: 🧩 Coordinate Conversion
docs.text:
The renderer uses helper functions:

logical_to_grid()
grid_to_logical()

These functions convert: - logical maze coordinates - expanded grid coordinates

This keeps rendering synchronized with: - BFS - DFS - gameplay movement

docs.title: 🚪 Door Rendering
docs.text:
The renderer calculates visual entry and exit doors using:

calculate_door_position()

This function: - determines which maze edge the door belongs to - offsets the position correctly - renders the external maze openings

docs.title: 🎞️ Animation System
docs.text: The project supports several animations.

docs.title: 🦆 Path Animation
docs.text:
Option 2 displays: - the shortest BFS path - the duck progressively moving through the maze

The animation progressively reveals:

game.path[:frame]

docs.title: 🌊 BFS Exploration Animation
docs.text:
Option 3 visualizes: - BFS traversal - explored cells - search progression

The animation uses:

game.explored[:frame]

to progressively display explored positions.

docs.title: 🚪 Exit Animation
docs.text:
When: - BFS finishes - the player reaches the exit

the exit portal becomes animated by alternating between:

assets.exit
assets.exit2

using timed frame switching.

docs.title: 🎮 Player Mode
docs.text:
Player mode allows real-time maze traversal using arrow keys.

Main function:

handle_player_movement()

Main features: - collision detection - smooth movement - trail rendering - backtracking - exit detection

docs.title: 🧱 Collision Detection
docs.text:
The player cannot move through: - walls (1) - logo blocks (2)

The movement system validates: - boundaries - blocked cells - valid traversal positions

before updating the player position.

docs.title: 👣 Player Trail System
docs.text:
The renderer stores the player path:

game.player_path

This allows: - visual backtracking - persistent player trails - movement visualization

When the player walks backwards: - the trail is removed dynamically

docs.title: 📜 Menu System
docs.text:
Main file:

render/menu.py

The menu system handles: - menu backgrounds - banner rendering - menu image loading - dynamic image generation

docs.title: 🖼️ Banner Rendering
docs.text:
The bottom banner acts as the game's UI.

It contains: - gameplay options - controls - theme information

The banner is rendered independently from the maze.

docs.title: ⚡ Rendering Loop
docs.text:
The MLX loop uses:

mlx.mlx_loop_hook()

This continuously: - redraws the screen - updates animations - refreshes gameplay state - synchronizes rendering

The project also uses:

mlx.mlx_do_sync()

to improve rendering consistency.

docs.title: 🧠 Rendering Goals
docs.text:
The rendering system was designed to: - provide real-time visualization - separate graphics from algorithms - support gameplay interaction - create animated algorithm demonstrations - dynamically scale assets - keep the project modular

The renderer acts as the visual layer between: - maze generation - gameplay systems - BFS/DFS algorithms - user interaction

docs.title: 📝 Evaluation Notes
docs.text: Common Born2beroot evaluation questions and short conceptual answers.

docs.title: What is a Virtual Machine (VM)?
docs.text:
A Virtual Machine is a virtual computer running inside a physical computer.

It behaves like a real machine and has its own operating system, memory, storage and network interfaces.

docs.title: What is a Hypervisor?
docs.text:
A Hypervisor is software that creates and manages virtual machines.

It allocates resources and allows multiple VMs to run on the same physical machine.

docs.title: What is VirtualBox?
docs.text:
VirtualBox is a Type 2 Hypervisor used to create and manage virtual machines.

It runs on top of an existing operating system.

docs.title: What is the difference between Host and Guest?
docs.text:
The Host is the real operating system running on the physical machine.

The Guest is the operating system running inside the virtual machine.

docs.title: What is Linux?
docs.text:
Linux is an operating system built around the Linux kernel.

It manages hardware resources and allows applications to run.

docs.title: What is the Kernel?
docs.text:
The Kernel is the core of the operating system.

It manages:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Hardware
  • Processes
  • Filesystems

docs.title: What is a Linux Distribution?
docs.text:
A Distribution combines:

  • Linux Kernel
  • Package Manager
  • Utilities
  • Configuration Tools

Examples include Debian and Rocky Linux.

docs.title: What is Root?
docs.text:
Root is the administrator account.

It has unrestricted access to the operating system.

docs.title: What is sudo?
docs.text:
sudo allows a user to execute commands with elevated privileges.

It provides temporary administrative access without logging directly as root.

docs.title: What is the difference between Root and sudo?
docs.text:
Root is the administrator account itself.

sudo is a mechanism that allows a user to temporarily use administrative privileges.

docs.title: What are Groups?
docs.text:
Groups allow multiple users to share permissions.

They simplify permission management.

docs.title: What is Ownership?
docs.text: Ownership determines which user and group control a file or directory.

docs.title: What is chmod?
docs.text: chmod is used to modify file and directory permissions.

docs.title: What is chown?
docs.text: chown is used to change file ownership.

docs.title: What is an IP Address?
docs.text:
An IP Address identifies a device on a network.

It allows devices to communicate with each other.

docs.title: What is DNS?
docs.text:
DNS converts human-readable names into IP addresses.

Example:

google.com → IP Address

docs.title: What is a Port?
docs.text: A Port identifies a specific network service running on a machine.

docs.title: What is SSH?
docs.text:
SSH (Secure Shell) allows secure remote access to another computer.

It encrypts communication between systems.

docs.title: What is TCP?
docs.text: TCP is a network protocol focused on reliability and ordered delivery of data.

docs.title: What is UDP?
docs.text: UDP is a network protocol focused on speed rather than guaranteed delivery.

docs.title: What is Authentication?
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

"Who are you?"

It verifies identity.

docs.title: What is Authorization?
docs.text:
Authorization answers:

"What are you allowed to do?"

It controls permissions.

docs.title: What is PAM?
docs.text:
PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) is Linux's authentication framework.

It centralizes authentication policies for services such as SSH, login and sudo.

docs.title: What is a Firewall?
docs.text:
A Firewall controls which network traffic is allowed or blocked.

It acts as a security barrier between systems.

docs.title: What is UFW?
docs.text: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a simplified tool used to manage firewall rules.

docs.title: What is AppArmor?
docs.text:
AppArmor is a security framework that restricts what applications are allowed to do.

It limits damage if an application becomes compromised.

docs.title: What is Least Privilege?
docs.text: Least Privilege means giving users and applications only the permissions they actually need.

docs.title: What is a Partition?
docs.text:
A Partition is a logical division of a disk.

It allows storage to be organized into separate sections.

docs.title: What is a Filesystem?
docs.text: A Filesystem defines how files are stored and organized on a disk.

docs.title: What is a Mount Point?
docs.text: A Mount Point is a directory where a filesystem becomes accessible.

docs.title: What is LVM?
docs.text: LVM (Logical Volume Manager) is a storage management system that provides flexible and resizable storage.

docs.title: What are PV, VG and LV?
docs.text:
PV (Physical Volume):

Storage managed by LVM.

VG (Volume Group):

A pool of storage created from one or more Physical Volumes.

LV (Logical Volume):

Virtual storage created from a Volume Group.

docs.title: What is Encryption?
docs.text:
Encryption converts readable data into protected data.

Without the correct key, the data cannot be understood.

docs.title: Why Encrypt Data?
docs.text: Encryption protects information if storage devices are lost, stolen or accessed without authorization.

docs.title: What is a Service?
docs.text: A Service is a program running in the background that provides functionality to the system.

docs.title: What is a Daemon?
docs.text: A Daemon is a background process that waits for work and usually starts automatically.

docs.title: What is systemd?
docs.text:
systemd is the service manager used by many Linux distributions.

It starts and manages services.

docs.title: What is systemctl?
docs.text: systemctl is the command-line tool used to interact with systemd.

docs.title: What is Logging?
docs.text: Logging is the process of recording system events.

docs.title: What is journald?
docs.text:
journald is the logging service used by systemd.

It collects system events and messages.

docs.title: What is journalctl?
docs.text: journalctl is used to view and search logs managed by journald.

docs.title: What is cron?
docs.text:
cron is Linux's task scheduler.

It runs commands automatically at scheduled times.

docs.title: What is Monitoring?
docs.text:
Monitoring is the process of observing system health and performance.

Examples include CPU, memory, storage and network usage.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is Linux?
docs.text:
Linux is an operating system.

An operating system sits between:

Hardware
    ↓
Operating System
    ↓
Applications

Without an operating system, applications would need to communicate directly with hardware.

Linux provides a stable and secure layer that allows software to run efficiently.

docs.title: 2️⃣ The Linux Philosophy
docs.text:
Linux follows a simple philosophy:

Do one thing and do it well

Many Linux tools are intentionally small and focused.

Examples:

  • grep
  • cat
  • find
  • sort
  • chmod

Each solves a specific problem.

docs.title: 3️⃣ What is the Kernel?
docs.text:
The kernel is the core of Linux.

Think of it as the operating system's manager.

Responsibilities include:

  • CPU scheduling
  • memory management
  • hardware communication
  • process management
  • filesystem access

docs.title: 4️⃣ User Space vs Kernel Space
docs.text: Linux separates the system into two worlds.

docs.title: User Space
docs.text:
Applications run here.

Examples:

  • Firefox
  • VSCode
  • Python

docs.title: Kernel Space
docs.text:
The kernel runs here.

Applications must ask permission before accessing hardware.

This separation improves security and stability.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Linux Distributions
docs.text:
Linux itself is only the kernel.

A distribution combines:

  • Linux kernel
  • package manager
  • utilities
  • configuration tools
  • documentation

Examples:

  • Debian
  • Ubuntu
  • Rocky Linux
  • Fedora
  • Arch Linux

docs.title: 6️⃣ Debian
docs.text:
Debian is one of the oldest and most respected Linux distributions.

Known for:

  • stability
  • reliability
  • large repositories
  • conservative updates

Many other distributions are based on Debian.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Rocky Linux
docs.text:
Rocky Linux focuses on enterprise environments.

Known for:

  • Red Hat compatibility
  • long-term support
  • server usage

It is commonly found in professional infrastructures.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Why So Many Distributions?
docs.text:
Different users have different goals.

Some prioritize:

  • stability
  • performance
  • security
  • ease of use
  • customization

This is why many Linux distributions exist.

docs.title: 9️⃣ The Linux Boot Process
docs.text:
A simplified boot sequence:

Power On
    ↓
BIOS / UEFI
    ↓
Bootloader
    ↓
Kernel
    ↓
systemd
    ↓
Services
    ↓
Login

Understanding this sequence helps explain how Linux starts.

docs.title: 🔟 BIOS and UEFI
docs.text:
These systems initialize hardware before Linux starts.

Responsibilities:

  • detect hardware
  • perform checks
  • locate boot devices

UEFI is the modern replacement for BIOS.

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Bootloaders
docs.text:
A bootloader loads the operating system.

One common example is:

GRUB

Its job is to locate and start the Linux kernel.

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ systemd
docs.text:
systemd is responsible for managing the system after the kernel starts.

It handles:

  • service startup
  • dependencies
  • logging
  • process supervision

Modern Linux distributions rely heavily on systemd.

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ The Shell
docs.text:
The shell is the interface between the user and the operating system.

You type commands:

ls
pwd
cd

The shell interprets them and communicates with the system.

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ Common Shells
docs.text:
Examples include:

  • Bash
  • Zsh
  • Fish
  • Dash

Bash remains the most widely known shell.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ Terminal vs Shell
docs.text: These terms are often confused.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text: The application window.

docs.title: Shell
docs.text:
The program running inside that window.

Example:

Terminal
    ↓
Bash

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ Commands and Utilities
docs.text:
Linux provides many small tools.

Examples:

ls
pwd
cat
grep
find

Combining small tools is one of Linux's greatest strengths.

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ Processes
docs.text:
A process is a running program.

Examples:

Python Script
Browser
SSH Server

Every running application becomes a process.

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Process Lifecycle
docs.text:
A process typically follows:

Created
   ↓
Running
   ↓
Waiting
   ↓
Finished

The kernel manages this lifecycle.

docs.title: Foreground
docs.text: Runs directly in the terminal.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Runs independently.

Examples include:

  • servers
  • monitoring services
  • daemons

docs.title: 2️⃣0️⃣ Process IDs (PID)
docs.text:
Every process receives a unique identifier.

Example:

PID 100
PID 250
PID 421

The kernel uses these IDs to manage processes.

docs.title: 2️⃣1️⃣ Files and Directories
docs.text:
Linux treats almost everything as a file.

Examples:

  • documents
  • devices
  • logs
  • configuration files

This creates a consistent environment.

docs.title: 2️⃣2️⃣ Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
docs.text:
Linux follows a standard structure.

/
├── home
├── etc
├── usr
├── var
├── boot
└── tmp

Everything starts from the root directory.

docs.title: /home
docs.text: User files.

docs.title: /etc
docs.text: Configuration files.

docs.title: /var
docs.text: Logs and changing data.

docs.title: /boot
docs.text: Boot-related files.

docs.title: /tmp
docs.text: Temporary files.

docs.title: 2️⃣4️⃣ Paths
docs.text:
Linux uses paths to locate files.

Example:

/home/student/document.txt

Paths can be:

  • absolute
  • relative

docs.title: 2️⃣5️⃣ Hidden Files
docs.text:
Files beginning with:

.

are hidden by default.

Examples:

.bashrc
.profile
.gitignore

docs.title: 2️⃣6️⃣ Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables store configuration values.

Examples:

PATH
HOME
USER
SHELL

Applications often rely on them.

docs.title: 2️⃣7️⃣ Package Managers
docs.text:
Package managers simplify software installation.

Examples:

  • apt
  • dnf
  • yum

They manage:

  • installation
  • updates
  • dependencies

docs.title: 2️⃣8️⃣ Why Linux Dominates Servers
docs.text:
Linux powers most servers because it offers:

✅ Stability

✅ Performance

✅ Security

✅ Flexibility

✅ Open-source development

Many cloud platforms rely heavily on Linux.

docs.title: 2️⃣9️⃣ Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of Linux as:

The operating system city

The kernel is:

The city manager

Processes are:

The citizens

The filesystem is:

The map

And the shell is:

Your way of communicating with the city

docs.title: 🔐 Security
docs.text: Understanding how Linux systems protect users, data and services.

docs.text:

  8. Authentication vs Authorization

  10. PAM
  11. PAM Workflow

  14. Common UFW Commands

  16. Attack Surface
  17. Hardening
  18. Security Layers
  19. Useful Commands

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is Security?
docs.text:
Security is the practice of protecting:

  • users
  • systems
  • applications
  • data

The goal is not:

Perfect Protection

because no system is completely secure.

The real goal is:

Reduce Risk

and limit damage when something goes wrong.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Security Matters
docs.text:
Imagine a Linux server connected to the internet.

Without security:

  • anyone could attempt access
  • services could be abused
  • data could be stolen
  • systems could be modified

Security exists to reduce those risks.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Security Principles
docs.text: Most security systems are built around a few important concepts.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: Give only the permissions that are required.

docs.title: Defense in Depth
docs.text: Use multiple layers of protection.

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text: Restrict who can access resources.

docs.title: Accountability
docs.text: Actions should be traceable.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Least Privilege
docs.text:
One of the most important security principles.

Example:

User only needs to read files

They should NOT receive:

  • write permissions
  • administrator privileges

Bad:

Everyone = Administrator

Good:

Each user receives only what is needed

Benefits:

✅ Smaller attack surface

✅ Fewer mistakes

✅ Better security

docs.title: 5️⃣ Defense in Depth
docs.text:
Never rely on a single protection layer.

Example:

Password
    ↓
Permissions
    ↓
Firewall
    ↓
AppArmor

If one layer fails, others still provide protection.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Examples:

  • Passwords
  • SSH Keys
  • Biometrics

Authentication verifies identity.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Examples:

  • Read files
  • Modify files
  • Install software

Authorization determines permissions.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text:
These concepts are often confused.

Authentication:

Identity Verification

Authorization:

Permission Verification

Example:

Login Successful
      ↓
Authentication
      ↓
Permission Check
      ↓
Authorization

docs.title: 9️⃣ Password Policies
docs.text:
Password policies define security rules.

Common requirements:

  • Minimum length
  • Complexity requirements
  • Expiration periods
  • Password history
  • Account lockouts

Example policy:

Minimum length: 10
Uppercase required
Lowercase required
Numbers required

Weak password:

password123

Stronger password:

Blue!Tiger84#Moon

docs.title: 🔟 PAM
docs.text:
PAM means:

Pluggable Authentication Modules

PAM is the authentication framework used by Linux.

Instead of every application implementing authentication separately:

SSH
sudo
login
   ↓
  PAM

all of them can share the same authentication rules.

Think of PAM as:

The central authentication manager

for the system.

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ PAM Workflow
docs.text:
Without PAM:

SSH
  ↓
Own Authentication Logic

sudo
  ↓
Own Authentication Logic

login
  ↓
Own Authentication Logic

With PAM:

SSH
sudo
login
   ↓
  PAM

Everything follows the same security policies.

PAM can enforce:

  • Password complexity
  • Password expiration
  • Account restrictions
  • Login limitations

Benefits:

✅ Centralized management

✅ Consistency

✅ Flexibility

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ UFW
docs.text:
UFW means:

Uncomplicated Firewall

UFW provides a simpler way to manage firewall rules.

Think of UFW as:

A security guard

standing at the entrance of a building.

Every connection request is checked.

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ Firewall Concepts
docs.text:
A firewall decides:

Allow?
or
Block?

for incoming and outgoing traffic.

Without a firewall:

Everything is exposed

With a firewall:

Only approved traffic passes

Example:

Internet
    ↓
Firewall
    ↓
Server

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ Common UFW Commands
docs.text:
View firewall status:

sudo ufw status

Allow SSH:

sudo ufw allow 22

Meaning:

Allow traffic to SSH

Deny traffic:

sudo ufw deny 80

Meaning:

Block traffic to HTTP

Enable firewall:

sudo ufw enable

These commands are examples for learning concepts.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ AppArmor
docs.text:
AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control system.

Its purpose is to restrict applications.

Example:

Web Server

Allowed:

/var/www

Not Allowed:

/home/user

Even if the application becomes compromised, AppArmor can limit damage.

Think of AppArmor as:

A set of invisible walls

around an application.

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ Attack Surface
docs.text:
Attack Surface means:

Everything an attacker can interact with

Examples:

  • Open ports
  • Running services
  • User accounts
  • Applications

Larger attack surface:

More opportunities for attacks

Smaller attack surface:

Fewer opportunities for attacks

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ Hardening
docs.text:
Hardening means:

Making a system more secure

Examples:

  • Disable unnecessary services
  • Restrict permissions
  • Configure firewalls
  • Use strong passwords
  • Reduce exposed ports

Hardening is proactive security.

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Security Layers
docs.text:
A secure system usually combines:

Passwords
      ↓
PAM
      ↓
Permissions
      ↓
Firewall
      ↓
AppArmor

No single mechanism should be trusted completely.

docs.title: 1️⃣9️⃣ Useful Commands
docs.text:
Current user:

whoami

User information:

id

File permissions:

ls -l

Firewall status:

sudo ufw status

Running services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Listening ports:

ss -tuln

These commands help administrators inspect the security state of a system.

docs.title: 2️⃣0️⃣ Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine a castle.

Authentication:

Who is at the gate?

Authorization:

Which rooms may they enter?

Firewall:

Outer Wall

PAM:

Identity Verification Process

AppArmor:

Internal Restrictions

Least Privilege:

Give only the keys that are needed

Final Mental Image

Authentication
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Permissions
      ↓
Firewall
      ↓
AppArmor
      ↓
Security

Security is the result of many protective layers working together.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is a Service?
docs.text:
A service is a program that runs in the background.

Unlike normal applications, services usually operate without direct user interaction.

Examples:

  • SSH Server
  • Database Server
  • Web Server

Think of a service as:

A worker operating behind the scenes

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Services Exist
docs.text:
Many tasks must continue running even when nobody is actively using the system.

Examples:

Website Hosting
Remote Access
Database Management

These functions are provided by services.

docs.title: 3️⃣ What is a Daemon?
docs.text:
In Linux, a background process is often called a:

Daemon

Examples:

sshd
cron
systemd-journald

A daemon usually starts automatically and waits for work.

Think of a daemon as:

A service always on standby

docs.title: 4️⃣ Services vs Applications
docs.text:
Applications:

User opens them

Examples:

  • Browser
  • VSCode
  • Calculator

Services:

Start automatically

and continue running in the background.

Example:

Browser → User launches

SSH Service → Runs continuously

docs.title: 5️⃣ What is systemd?
docs.text:
systemd is one of the most important Linux components.

After Linux boots, systemd becomes responsible for managing the system.

Responsibilities include:

  • Starting services
  • Stopping services
  • Monitoring services
  • Managing dependencies
  • Collecting logs

Think of systemd as:

The operating system manager

docs.title: 6️⃣ Why systemd Exists
docs.text:
Before systemd, Linux distributions used different startup systems.

Managing services was often inconsistent.

systemd introduced:

✅ Standardization

✅ Faster startup

✅ Better service management

✅ Centralized logging

docs.title: 7️⃣ Service Lifecycle
docs.text:
A service typically follows:

Stopped
   ↓
Started
   ↓
Running
   ↓
Stopped

Some services restart automatically if they fail.

docs.title: 8️⃣ systemctl
docs.text:
systemctl is the command-line tool used to communicate with systemd.

Think of it as:

The remote control for services

docs.title: 9️⃣ Common systemctl Commands
docs.text:
Display service status:

systemctl status ssh

Start a service:

sudo systemctl start ssh

Stop a service:

sudo systemctl stop ssh

Restart a service:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

Enable automatic startup:

sudo systemctl enable ssh

List running services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

These examples are provided to explain concepts.

docs.title: 🔟 What is Logging?
docs.text:
Logs are records of events occurring on a system.

Think of logs as:

A system diary

Logs help answer questions such as:

  • What happened?
  • When did it happen?
  • Why did it happen?

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Why Logs Matter
docs.text:
Without logs:

Troubleshooting becomes guesswork

Logs help identify:

  • errors
  • crashes
  • failed logins
  • service failures
  • security incidents

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ journald
docs.text:
journald is the logging service provided by systemd.

It collects events from across the operating system.

Examples:

  • Service messages
  • Startup events
  • Errors
  • Warnings

Think of journald as:

The central log collector

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ journalctl
docs.text:
journalctl is used to read logs managed by journald.

Think of it as:

A search tool for system events

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ Common journalctl Commands
docs.text:
Display recent logs:

journalctl

Display logs for a service:

journalctl -u ssh

Display latest entries:

journalctl -n 50

Display logs from current boot:

journalctl -b

These commands help administrators investigate problems.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ Cron
docs.text:
Cron is Linux's scheduling system.

It allows commands and scripts to run automatically.

Examples:

  • Backups
  • Monitoring
  • Reports
  • Maintenance tasks

Think of cron as:

A task scheduler

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ Why Automation Matters
docs.text:
Many administrative tasks repeat regularly.

Without automation:

Humans must remember everything

Automation improves:

  • consistency
  • reliability
  • efficiency

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ Monitoring
docs.text:
Monitoring means observing system health.

Administrators monitor:

  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Disk usage
  • Network activity
  • Running services

Monitoring answers:

Is the system healthy?

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Resource Monitoring
docs.text: Important resources include:

docs.title: CPU
docs.text: Processing power.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: RAM usage.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Disk capacity.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Traffic and connectivity.

Problems often appear first in monitoring data.

docs.title: 1️⃣9️⃣ Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
Linux provides many monitoring tools.

Examples:

  • top
  • htop
  • free
  • df
  • uptime

Each focuses on a different aspect of system health.

docs.title: 2️⃣0️⃣ Common Monitoring Commands
docs.text:
View running processes:

top

Display memory usage:

free -h

Display disk usage:

df -h

Display system uptime:

uptime

Display process information:

ps aux

These commands provide insight into system performance.

docs.title: 2️⃣1️⃣ Troubleshooting Mindset
docs.text:
When something breaks, administrators usually ask:

  • Is the service running?
  • What do the logs say?
  • Is the system overloaded?
  • Did anything change recently?

Common troubleshooting flow:

Problem
   ↓
Check Service
   ↓
Check Logs
   ↓
Check Resources
   ↓
Find Cause

Good troubleshooting relies on evidence rather than guesses.

docs.title: 2️⃣2️⃣ Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine a city.

Services are:

Workers

Daemons are:

Workers always on duty

systemd is:

The city manager

journald is:

The city recorder

journalctl is:

The archive search system

cron is:

The scheduler

Monitoring tools are:

Security cameras

Final Mental Image

systemd
    ↓
Services
    ↓
Logs
    ↓
Monitoring
    ↓
Troubleshooting

Understanding these concepts is essential for maintaining healthy Linux systems.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why Storage Matters
docs.text:
Every operating system needs a place to store:

  • files
  • applications
  • configuration
  • logs
  • user data

Without storage, all information would disappear when the computer shuts down.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Physical Disks
docs.text:
Storage begins with a physical device.

Examples:

  • HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
  • SSD (Solid State Drive)
  • NVMe SSD

Linux sees these devices as storage resources that can be organized and divided.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Disk Layout
docs.text:
Think of a disk as a completely empty piece of land.

Entire Disk
┌───────────────────┐
│                   │
│    Empty Space    │
│                   │
└───────────────────┘

Before it can be used efficiently, it is usually divided into sections.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Partitions
docs.text:
A partition is a logical division of a disk.

Example:

Disk
├── Partition 1
├── Partition 2
└── Partition 3

Each partition behaves almost like an independent storage area.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Why Use Partitions?
docs.text:
Partitions provide:

✅ Organization

✅ Isolation

✅ Easier management

✅ Better security

Example:

Partition 1 → System
Partition 2 → User Files
Partition 3 → Logs

If one partition fills up, the others remain unaffected.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Filesystems
docs.text:
A filesystem defines how data is stored and organized.

Without a filesystem:

Disk = Raw Storage

Linux would not know how to manage files.

Common filesystems:

  • ext4
  • XFS
  • Btrfs

Think of a filesystem as:

The filing system of a library

It determines where everything is stored.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Mount Points
docs.text:
Linux does not assign drive letters like Windows.

Instead, storage is attached to directories.

This process is called:

Mounting

Example:

Storage Device
      ↓
Mount Point
      ↓
/home

docs.title: 8️⃣ The Linux Filesystem Tree
docs.text:
Linux has a single directory tree.

Everything starts at:

/

called:

Root Directory

Example:

/
├── home
├── var
├── boot
└── etc

Additional storage is attached somewhere inside this tree.

docs.title: /home
docs.text: User files.

docs.title: /var
docs.text: Logs and changing data.

docs.title: /boot
docs.text: Boot-related files.

Root filesystem.

Example:

Disk A
   ↓
/

Disk B
   ↓
/home

docs.title: 🔟 What Happens During Boot?
docs.text:
When Linux starts:

  1. Detect storage
  2. Load filesystems
  3. Mount partitions
  4. Make data available

Only after mounting can files be accessed.

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ LVM Introduction
docs.text:
LVM means:

Logical Volume Manager

This is one of the most important Born2beroot concepts.

Many students struggle with it because it adds an extra layer between the disk and the filesystem.

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ Why LVM Exists
docs.text:
Traditional partitions are rigid.

Example:

Partition = 20 GB

If it becomes full, resizing may be difficult.

LVM introduces flexibility.

Instead of thinking about fixed partitions:

Think about storage pools

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ Physical Volumes
docs.text:
A Physical Volume (PV) is storage managed by LVM.

Example:

Disk
   ↓
Physical Volume

Think of a PV as raw storage that LVM can use.

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ Volume Groups
docs.text:
A Volume Group (VG) combines storage.

Example:

PV1 = 100 GB
PV2 = 100 GB

VG = 200 GB

Multiple disks can be combined into a single storage pool.

This is one of LVM's biggest advantages.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ Logical Volumes
docs.text:
Logical Volumes (LVs) are created from the Volume Group.

Example:

Volume Group
     ↓
 ├── LV Home
 ├── LV Root
 └── LV Logs

To Linux, these behave similarly to partitions.

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ LVM Workflow
docs.text:
The easiest way to remember LVM:

Disk
  ↓
Physical Volume (PV)
  ↓
Volume Group (VG)
  ↓
Logical Volume (LV)
  ↓
Filesystem

Or visually:

Disk
 │
 ▼
PV
 │
 ▼
VG
 │
 ▼
LV
 │
 ▼
ext4

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ LVM Advantages
docs.text:
Benefits include:

✅ Easier resizing

✅ Flexible storage

✅ Better management

✅ Storage pooling

Example:

Traditional partition:

20 GB

Needs more space?

Often difficult.

LVM:

20 GB
      ↓
40 GB

Usually much easier to expand.

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Encryption
docs.text:
Encryption protects stored data.

Without the correct key:

Data remains unreadable

Encryption converts:

Readable Data

into:

Protected Data

docs.title: 1️⃣9️⃣ Why Encrypt Data?
docs.text:
Imagine someone steals a hard drive.

Without encryption:

Files may be readable

With encryption:

Files appear meaningless

without the correct credentials.

Benefits:

✅ Privacy

✅ Security

✅ Theft protection

docs.title: 2️⃣0️⃣ LUKS Concepts
docs.text:
LUKS is commonly used for disk encryption on Linux.

Think of it as:

A lock protecting storage

Example:

Disk
   ↓
LUKS
   ↓
Filesystem

Before data can be accessed, the lock must be opened.

docs.title: 2️⃣1️⃣ Storage Commands
docs.text:
Display disks:

df -h

Display filesystem usage:

du -sh folder

Display partition information:

fdisk -l

mount

Display LVM information:

pvs
vgs
lvs

These commands help administrators understand storage layout.

docs.title: 2️⃣2️⃣ Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine a shopping center.

The disk is:

The entire building

Partitions are:

Individual stores

Filesystems are:

The organization system
inside each store

LVM is:

A manager capable of
expanding or shrinking stores
when needed

Encryption is:

A lock on the building

Disk

Partition

Filesystem
  ↓
Mount Point

Traditional storage.

Disk

PV

VG

docs.title: 👤 Users and Permissions
docs.text: Understanding how Linux manages users, groups, ownership and access control.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why Users Exist
docs.text:
Linux was designed as a multi-user operating system.

Without users and permissions:

Everyone could access everything

which would be a major security risk.

Users allow Linux to identify:

  • who is performing an action
  • who owns a file
  • who can access a resource

docs.title: 2️⃣ Users
docs.text:
A user represents an identity inside Linux.

Examples:

sara
student
admin

Users can:

  • own files
  • run processes
  • belong to groups
  • access resources

Every action performed on Linux is associated with a user.

docs.title: Viewing Current User
docs.text:
whoami

Displays the current logged-in user.

Example:

sara

docs.title: Viewing User Information
docs.text:
id

Displays:

  • User ID (UID)
  • Group ID (GID)
  • Group memberships

Example:

uid=1000(sara)
gid=1000(sara)
groups=1000(sara),27(sudo)

docs.title: 3️⃣ Groups
docs.text:
Groups allow permissions to be assigned to multiple users simultaneously.

Instead of managing:

Sara
John
Maria

individually, Linux can use:

developers

and assign permissions to the group.

docs.title: Viewing Groups
docs.text:
groups

Displays groups associated with the current user.

docs.title: Creating Groups
docs.text:
groupadd developers

Creates a new group.

docs.title: Adding Users to Groups
docs.text:
usermod -aG developers sara

Adds a user to a group.

docs.title: Why Groups Matter
docs.text:
Groups simplify permission management.

Instead of assigning permissions individually, permissions can be assigned once to a group.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Root User
docs.text:
Root is the administrator account.

Root has unrestricted access.

Root can:

  • install software
  • create users
  • remove users
  • modify system configuration
  • change permissions

Think of root as:

The owner of the entire system

docs.title: 5️⃣ Sudo
docs.text:
Instead of logging directly as root, Linux commonly uses:

sudo command

Example:

sudo apt update

Sudo allows:

Temporary administrator privileges

Benefits:

  • accountability
  • logging
  • better security

docs.title: 6️⃣ Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text: These concepts are different.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Answers:

Who are you?

Examples:

  • Passwords
  • SSH Keys

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Examples:

  • Read files
  • Modify files
  • Install software

Authentication identifies.

Authorization grants permissions.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Ownership
docs.text:
Every file has:

  • an owner
  • a group owner

Example:

Owner: sara
Group: developers

Ownership determines who controls the resource.

docs.title: Viewing Ownership
docs.text:
ls -l

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 sara developers file.txt

docs.title: 8️⃣ Permission Model
docs.text:
Linux uses three permission categories.

Owner
Group
Others

Each category receives different permissions.

docs.title: 9️⃣ Read, Write and Execute
docs.text: Linux permissions are built around three actions.

docs.title: Read (r)
docs.text:
Allows viewing content.

Examples:

  • open files
  • view directories

docs.title: Write (w)
docs.text:
Allows modifications.

Examples:

  • edit files
  • create files
  • delete files

docs.title: Execute (x)
docs.text:
Allows execution.

Examples:

  • run programs
  • run shell scripts

docs.title: 🔟 Viewing Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

-rwxr-xr--

Breakdown:

rwx | r-x | r--

Owner | Group | Others

Meaning:

Owner:

  • Read
  • Write
  • Execute

Group:

  • Read
  • Execute

Others:

  • Read

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ chmod
docs.text:
chmod means:

Change Mode

Used to modify permissions.

Example:

chmod 755 script.sh

Changes file permissions.

Making a script executable:

chmod +x script.sh

One of the most common uses of chmod.

Removing write permission:

chmod -w file.txt

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ Numeric Permissions
docs.text:
Linux can represent permissions numerically.

Common values:

755
744
700
644

Relationship:

r = 4
w = 2
x = 1

Examples:

7 = rwx
6 = rw-
5 = r-x
4 = r--

Example:

chmod 644 file.txt

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ Symbolic Permissions
docs.text:
Instead of numbers, permissions can be modified symbolically.

Examples:

chmod +x script.sh
chmod -w file.txt
chmod g+w file.txt

Symbolic mode focuses on:

Adding or removing permissions

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ chown
docs.text:
chown means:

Change Owner

Used to transfer ownership.

Example:

chown sara file.txt

Changes the owner.

Changing owner and group:

chown sara:developers file.txt

Ownership and permissions work together.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ Useful User Commands
docs.text:
Display current user:

whoami

Display user information:

id

Create a user:

useradd username

Delete a user:

userdel username

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ Useful Group Commands
docs.text:
Display groups:

groups

Create group:

groupadd developers

Modify group membership:

usermod -aG developers sara

Delete group:

groupdel developers

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ Security Principles
docs.text: Linux permissions follow important security concepts.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: Give users only the permissions they need.

docs.title: Separation of Responsibilities
docs.text: Different users perform different tasks.

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
Protect resources according to their importance.

Permissions are one of Linux's primary security mechanisms.

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine an office building.

Users are:

Employees

Groups are:

Departments

Files are:

Documents

Permissions are:

Access badges

Root is:

The building owner

Final Mental Image

Users
    ↓
Groups
    ↓
Permissions
    ↓
Security

Linux uses this hierarchy to control who can access what.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is Virtualization?
docs.text:
Virtualization is the process of creating a virtual version of a computer system.

Instead of running a single operating system directly on physical hardware, virtualization allows multiple isolated systems to run on the same machine.

Think of virtualization as:

Creating a computer inside another computer

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Virtualization Exists
docs.text:
Before virtualization became common, organizations typically used:

1 Physical Server
        =
1 Operating System

This approach caused several problems:

  • Expensive hardware
  • Low resource usage
  • Difficult maintenance
  • Poor scalability

Many servers used only a small percentage of their available resources.

Example:

CPU Usage: 10%
RAM Usage: 15%
Disk Usage: 20%

Most of the hardware remained unused.

Virtualization was created to solve this problem.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Physical Machines Before Virtualization
docs.text:
Traditional infrastructure looked like this:

Server A → Database
Server B → Website
Server C → Mail Server
Server D → Backup System

Each service required its own machine.

Today, a single powerful server can host many virtual systems simultaneously.

docs.title: 4️⃣ What is a Virtual Machine?
docs.text:
A Virtual Machine (VM) behaves like a completely independent computer.

A VM has:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Storage
  • Network Interface
  • Operating System

Even though these resources are virtual, the operating system treats them as real hardware.

Example:

Physical Machine
      │
      ▼
 Hypervisor
      │
      ▼
 Virtual Machine
      │
      ▼
 Debian Linux

docs.title: 5️⃣ Hypervisors
docs.text:
A hypervisor is software responsible for managing virtual machines.

Its job is to:

  • Create virtual machines
  • Allocate resources
  • Isolate systems
  • Control access to hardware

Without a hypervisor, virtualization would not be possible.

Popular hypervisors:

  • VirtualBox
  • VMware
  • Hyper-V
  • KVM
  • Xen

docs.title: 6️⃣ Type 1 vs Type 2 Hypervisors
docs.text: There are two main categories.

docs.title: Type 1 Hypervisors
docs.text:
Run directly on hardware.

Hardware
    │
Hypervisor
    │
Virtual Machines

Examples:

  • VMware ESXi
  • Hyper-V Server
  • Xen

docs.title: Type 2 Hypervisors
docs.text:
Run inside another operating system.

Hardware
    │
Host OS
    │
VirtualBox
    │
Virtual Machines

Examples:

  • VirtualBox
  • VMware Workstation

Born2beroot normally uses this model.

docs.title: 7️⃣ VirtualBox Overview
docs.text:
VirtualBox is one of the most popular desktop virtualization tools.

It allows users to:

  • Create VMs
  • Allocate resources
  • Manage virtual disks
  • Create snapshots
  • Configure networking

VirtualBox acts as the bridge between the host machine and the guest operating system.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Host vs Guest Systems
docs.text: This distinction is extremely important.

docs.title: Host
docs.text:
The host is:

The real machine

Examples:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux

docs.title: Guest
docs.text:
The guest is:

The virtual machine

Examples:

  • Debian
  • Rocky Linux

Example:

Windows Host
      │
VirtualBox
      │
Debian Guest

docs.title: 9️⃣ Virtual Hardware
docs.text:
Every VM receives virtual hardware.

Examples:

  • Virtual CPU
  • Virtual RAM
  • Virtual Disk
  • Virtual Network Card

The guest operating system believes this hardware is real.

docs.title: 🔟 Virtual CPU
docs.text:
The virtual CPU represents processing power assigned to the VM.

Example:

Physical CPU = 8 cores

VM 1 = 2 cores
VM 2 = 2 cores
VM 3 = 2 cores
VM 4 = 2 cores

The hypervisor distributes resources between machines.

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Virtual RAM
docs.text:
Memory is also shared.

Example:

Physical RAM = 16 GB

VM A = 4 GB
VM B = 4 GB
VM C = 4 GB

Allocating too much memory may negatively impact the host system.

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ Virtual Storage
docs.text:
A VM stores data inside virtual disks.

The guest operating system sees:

A normal hard drive

even though the disk is actually a file on the host machine.

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ Virtual Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Virtual machines require network connectivity.

Virtual adapters allow:

  • Internet access
  • Communication between VMs
  • Communication with the host

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ Virtual Disks
docs.text:
Virtual disks are files representing storage devices.

Common formats:

  • VDI
  • VHD
  • VMDK

The guest system treats these files as physical disks.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ Snapshots
docs.text:
Snapshots are one of the most useful virtualization features.

A snapshot records the state of a VM at a specific moment.

Example:

Clean Installation
      ↓
Snapshot
      ↓
Experiment
      ↓
Problem Occurs
      ↓
Restore Snapshot

Snapshots make testing much safer.

docs.title: 1️⃣6️⃣ Resource Allocation
docs.text:
Every VM consumes resources.

Administrators must decide:

  • CPU allocation
  • Memory allocation
  • Storage allocation
  • Network configuration

Poor allocation can reduce performance.

docs.title: 1️⃣7️⃣ Advantages of Virtualization
docs.text:
Benefits include:

✅ Isolation

✅ Easy testing

✅ Portability

✅ Lower hardware costs

✅ Better resource utilization

✅ Safer experimentation

docs.title: 1️⃣8️⃣ Disadvantages of Virtualization
docs.text:
Potential drawbacks:

❌ Resource overhead

❌ Increased complexity

❌ Additional management layers

❌ Hardware limitations

Despite these drawbacks, the benefits usually outweigh the costs.

docs.title: 1️⃣9️⃣ Real World Uses
docs.text:
Virtualization is used almost everywhere.

Examples:

  • Cloud providers
  • Development environments
  • Testing platforms
  • Corporate servers
  • Educational environments

Companies often run hundreds or thousands of virtual machines.

docs.title: 2️⃣0️⃣ Virtualization vs Containers
docs.text: Students often confuse these concepts.

docs.title: Virtual Machines
docs.text:
Include:

Operating System
Kernel
Applications

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Share the host kernel.

They are lighter and faster but provide a different type of isolation.

Examples:

  • Docker
  • Podman
