docs.title: 1. What is MLX?
docs.text:
MinilibX (MLX) is a minimal graphical library created by Olivier Crouzet for 42 school students. Its entire purpose is to let you open a window, draw pixels in it, load images, and react to keyboard and mouse events — without needing to know Vulkan, X11, or any other low-level graphics system.

It is intentionally small. It does not provide: - Text rendering beyond a basic fixed-size bitmap font - Audio - 3D or GPU shaders (the GPU is used internally, but not exposed) - Menus, widgets, or UI components - Networking or remote display

Everything beyond these basics is for you to build.

The Python version (mlx_CLXV 2.2) is a ctypes wrapper around the C library (libmlx.so). Every Python method maps directly to a C function with the same name.

docs.title: 2. How it Works (Architecture)
docs.text:
Your Python Code
      │
      ▼
  Mlx class (mlx.py)        ← Python ctypes wrapper
      │
      ▼
  libmlx.so                 ← compiled C library
      │
      ├── XCB backend       ← talks to the X server (window, events)
      └── Vulkan backend    ← GPU drawing (pixels, images, text)

The main loop (mlx_loop) is an infinite event loop inside the C library. It: - Waits for events (key presses, mouse clicks, window events) - Calls your registered Python callback functions when those events occur - Calls your loop hook function on every iteration when no other event is pending

Your program must register hooks before calling mlx_loop. Once inside the loop, your code only runs when a hook fires.

docs.title: 3. Getting Started
docs.text:
Minimum working program:

from mlx import Mlx
import os

def on_key(key, param):
    if key == 65307:  # ESC
        os._exit(0)

mlx = Mlx()
mlx_ptr = mlx.mlx_init()
win_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, 800, 600, "My Window")

mlx.mlx_key_hook(win_ptr, on_key, None)
mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 33, 0, lambda p: os._exit(0), None)  # close button

mlx.mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)

docs.title: mlx_init()
docs.text:
mlx_ptr = mlx.mlx_init()

Must be called first, before anything else. Creates the connection to the display system (XCB + Vulkan).

  • Returns: connection identifier (void *) — pass this to most other functions
  • Returns None on failure

docs.title: mlx_release(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_release(mlx_ptr)

Disconnects from the display and frees all internal resources. Call this at the end of your program after the loop exits.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, width, height, title)
docs.text:
win_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, 1600, 900, "A-MAZE-ING")

Creates a new window on screen. MLX can manage multiple windows simultaneously — each call creates a separate window.

  • width: window width in pixels
  • height: window height in pixels
  • title: text shown in the window's title bar (string, auto-encoded to UTF-8)
  • Returns: window identifier — pass this to drawing and hook functions
  • Returns None on failure

Origin (0, 0) is the top-left corner. X increases right, Y increases downward.

docs.title: mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)

Fills the entire window with black (0x000000). Use this to erase everything before redrawing each frame.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_destroy_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_destroy_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)

Closes and destroys the window. The window identifier becomes invalid after this call. Useful when managing multiple windows and you want to close just one.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_pixel_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, x, y, color)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_pixel_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, 100, 200, 0xFFFFFFFF)

Draws a single pixel at position (x, y) with the given color. This is the most basic drawing primitive.

  • x, y: pixel coordinates (top-left origin)
  • color: unsigned int, format 0xAARRGGBB (see Color section)
  • Returns: 0 on success

Warning: mlx_pixel_put is slow because it sends each pixel individually to the GPU. For anything beyond a few pixels, use images instead.

docs.title: mlx_string_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, x, y, color, string)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_string_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, 100, 50, 0xFFFFFFFF, "Hello World")

Renders a text string at position (x, y) using MLX's built-in bitmap font.

  • x, y: position of the top-left of the first character
  • color: text color as unsigned int (only RGB used, alpha is forced to 255)
  • string: the text to display (auto-encoded to UTF-8)
  • Returns: 0 on success

Font details: - Fixed-size bitmap font (same font on all platforms using this MLX version) - Supports ASCII characters 32–127 (space through ~) - Characters outside that range display as a placeholder - You cannot change the font size or font face - Approximately 7–8 pixels wide per character, ~13 pixels tall

What you can do with text: - Change color to anything (white, yellow, red, etc.) - Position it anywhere in the window - Draw it on top of images (images drawn after will cover it) - Create simple labels, counters, status text

What you cannot do: - Change font size - Use bold/italic - Get the pixel width of a string (estimate ~7–8 px per char)

docs.title: 7. Images
docs.text: Images are the recommended way to draw in MLX. Instead of sending pixel-by-pixel to the GPU, you build an image in memory then send the whole thing at once.

docs.title: mlx_new_image(mlx_ptr, width, height)
docs.text:
img_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_image(mlx_ptr, 200, 200)

Creates a blank image in memory of the given size.

  • Returns: image identifier, or None on failure

docs.title: mlx_get_data_addr(img_ptr)
docs.text:
data, bits_per_pixel, size_line, img_format = mlx.mlx_get_data_addr(img_ptr)

Returns a writable memoryview of the image's raw pixel data, plus metadata. This is the key function for drawing into images.

  • data: memoryview (cast to 'B') — writable byte buffer of the image
  • bits_per_pixel: how many bits represent one pixel (typically 32)
  • size_line: number of bytes per row of the image
  • img_format:
  • 0 = B8G8R8A8 byte order
  • 1 = A8R8G8B8 byte order

Writing a single pixel into an image:

def put_pixel(data, size_line, x, y, color_bytes):
    offset = y * size_line + x * 4
    data[offset:offset + 4] = color_bytes

# Example: white pixel at (10, 20)
put_pixel(data, size_line, 10, 20, (0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF))

Filling the whole image with one color:

color = (0xFF, 0x00, 0x00, 0xFF)  # red, fully opaque
for offset in range(0, size_line * height, 4):
    data[offset:offset + 4] = color

docs.title: mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_ptr, x, y)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_ptr, 0, 0)

Renders an image onto the window at position (x, y). The image's top-left corner lands at (x, y). Images drawn later will appear on top of earlier ones.

  • x, y: can be negative (image partially off-screen is fine)
  • Returns: 0 on success

This is fast — it sends the whole image buffer to the GPU in one call.

docs.title: mlx_destroy_image(mlx_ptr, img_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_destroy_image(mlx_ptr, img_ptr)

Frees the memory for an image. Always destroy images you no longer need to avoid memory leaks.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_xpm_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, filename)
docs.text:
img_ptr, width, height = mlx.mlx_xpm_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, "assets/wall.xpm")

Loads an XPM file and creates an image from it. XPM is the recommended format for this MLX version — it is the most reliable loader.

  • filename: path to the .xpm file (string, auto-encoded)
  • Returns: tuple (img_ptr, width, height)
  • img_ptr is None on failure
  • Supports transparency in XPM

XPM files can be generated from PNG using ImageMagick: 

magick input.png output.xpm

docs.title: mlx_png_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, filename)
docs.text:
img_ptr, width, height = mlx.mlx_png_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, "assets/wall.png")

Loads a PNG file and creates an image from it.

  • Returns: tuple (img_ptr, width, height)
  • img_ptr is None on failure

Warning: The PNG loader in this MLX version is incomplete and unreliable on some systems/PNG types. Prefer XPM for production use — convert PNGs to XPM first with ImageMagick.

docs.title: mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)  # ← program runs here until exit

Starts the infinite event loop. This call never returns under normal operation. The program now runs entirely through callbacks registered with the various hook functions.

  • Must be called after all hooks are registered
  • All windows, images, and hooks must be set up before this call
  • Returns only if mlx_loop_exit is called from within a callback

Note for Python: You cannot catch Ctrl+C (SIGINT) while inside mlx_loop. Use Ctrl+\ (SIGQUIT) to force-kill the process, or call os._exit(0) from within a key hook.

docs.title: mlx_loop_exit(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_loop_exit(mlx_ptr)

Signals the event loop to stop. mlx_loop will return after this is called. Use this for clean shutdown instead of os._exit(0) when you want code to run after the loop (resource cleanup, etc.).

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_key_hook(win_ptr, callback, param)
docs.text:
def on_key(keycode, param):
    print(f"Key released: {keycode}")

mlx.mlx_key_hook(win_ptr, on_key, None)

Registers a function to call when a key is released (KeyRelease event, not KeyPress).

  • callback: function with signature (keycode: int, param: any) -> None
  • param: any Python object, passed back to the callback unchanged
  • Returns: 0 on success

To disable the hook: 

mlx.mlx_key_hook(win_ptr, None, None)

Common key codes (Linux/XCB):

Key Code Key Code ESC 65307 Space 32 Enter 65293 Tab 65289 Up arrow 65362 Down 65364 Left 65361 Right 65363 a 97 z 122 0 48 9 57 1 49 2 50 F1 65470 F12 65481 Backspace 65288 Delete 65535 Shift (L) 65505 Ctrl (L) 65507

Find any key code by printing it: print(f"Key: {keycode}")

docs.title: mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, callback, param)
docs.text:
def on_mouse(button, x, y, param):
    print(f"Button {button} clicked at ({x}, {y})")

mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, on_mouse, None)

Registers a function to call when a mouse button is pressed.

  • callback: function with signature (button: int, x: int, y: int, param: any) -> None
  • button: which button was clicked (see below)
  • x, y: coordinates of the click inside the window (top-left origin)
  • param: any Python object, passed back unchanged
  • Returns: 0 on success

Mouse button codes:

Button Code Left click 1 Middle click 2 Right click 3 Scroll up 4 Scroll down 5

To disable the hook: 

mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, None, None)

Hit-test example (clickable button area):

BTN_X, BTN_Y, BTN_W, BTN_H = 100, 200, 240, 55

def on_mouse(button, x, y, param):
    if button == 1:
        if BTN_X <= x <= BTN_X + BTN_W and BTN_Y <= y <= BTN_Y + BTN_H:
            print("Button clicked!")

mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, on_mouse, None)

docs.title: mlx_expose_hook(win_ptr, callback, param)
docs.text:
def on_expose(param):
    state.needs_redraw = True

mlx.mlx_expose_hook(win_ptr, on_expose, None)

Registers a function to call when a window needs to be redrawn (e.g., after being uncovered by another window or after alt-tab).

  • callback: function with signature (param: any) -> None
  • Returns: 0 on success

Important: On modern Linux with Wayland or X11 with compositing, this event may only fire once at program start (or never). The X server often saves the window content itself. Always re-draw from your loop_hook using a dirty flag pattern instead of relying solely on expose.

docs.title: mlx_loop_hook(mlx_ptr, callback, param)
docs.text:
def on_loop(param):
    if state.needs_redraw:
        mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
        draw_everything()
        state.needs_redraw = False

mlx.mlx_loop_hook(mlx_ptr, on_loop, None)

Registers a function that is called on every iteration of the event loop when no other event is pending. This is the primary place for your rendering logic.

  • callback: function with signature (param: any) -> None
  • Not bound to a window — bound to the mlx_ptr connection
  • Returns: 0 on success

Recommended pattern — dirty flag:

state.needs_redraw = True  # set to True whenever something changes

def on_loop(param):
    if not state.needs_redraw:
        return  # nothing to do, skip this frame
    mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
    # ... draw ...
    state.needs_redraw = False

This avoids redrawing 60+ times per second when nothing has changed.

docs.title: mlx_hook(win_ptr, x_event, x_mask, callback, param)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 33, 0, on_close, None)

The most powerful hook — lets you listen to any X11 event type, not just the three covered by the convenience hooks.

  • x_event: X11 event number (see table below)
  • x_mask: X11 event mask (usually 0 for modern MLX; masks are often ignored)
  • callback: function — signature depends on the event type (see below)
  • Returns: 0 on success

X11 Event Numbers (most useful):

x_event Name When it fires Callback signature 2 KeyPress Key held down (before release) (keycode, param) 3 KeyRelease Key released (same as key_hook) (keycode, param) 4 ButtonPress Mouse button pressed (button, x, y, param) 5 ButtonRelease Mouse button released (button, x, y, param) 6 MotionNotify Mouse moved while button held (x, y, param) 7 EnterNotify Mouse cursor enters the window (param) 8 LeaveNotify Mouse cursor leaves the window (param) 12 Expose Window needs redraw (same as expose_hook) (param) 33 ClientMessage Window close button (X button) clicked (param)

Key difference from convenience hooks: - mlx_key_hook → fires on KeyRelease (3) - mlx_hook(win, 2, ...) → fires on KeyPress, useful for detecting key held down

Mouse motion (hover) example:

def on_motion(x, y, param):
    # x, y = current mouse position inside window
    # Use this to implement hover effects
    if BTN_X <= x <= BTN_X + BTN_W and BTN_Y <= y <= BTN_Y + BTN_H:
        state.hovering = True
    else:
        state.hovering = False
    state.needs_redraw = True

mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 6, 0, on_motion, None)

Note: Event 6 (MotionNotify) only fires when a mouse button is held while moving. If you want mouse position tracking without a button held, poll mlx_mouse_get_pos in your loop hook instead.

Mouse enter/leave window example:

def on_enter(param):
    state.mouse_in_window = True

def on_leave(param):
    state.mouse_in_window = False

mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 7, 0, on_enter, None)
mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 8, 0, on_leave, None)

docs.title: mlx_mouse_hide(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_mouse_hide(mlx_ptr)

Hides the system mouse cursor. The cursor becomes invisible inside the window. Useful for games where you draw your own custom cursor as an image.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_mouse_show(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_mouse_show(mlx_ptr)

Makes the system mouse cursor visible again after mlx_mouse_hide.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_mouse_move(mlx_ptr, x, y)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_mouse_move(mlx_ptr, 400, 300)

Programmatically moves the mouse cursor to position (x, y) inside the window. Useful to snap the cursor to a specific location.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr) — returns tuple
docs.text:
ret, x, y = mlx.mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr)

Returns the current mouse cursor position without waiting for a click event. Useful for hover effects when polled from the loop hook.

  • Returns: tuple (ret, x, y)
  • x, y: current cursor position in the window
  • ret: 0 on success

Hover effect using poll (no button needed):

def on_loop(param):
    _, x, y = mlx.mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr)
    hovering = BTN_X <= x <= BTN_X + BTN_W and BTN_Y <= y <= BTN_Y + BTN_H
    if hovering != state.last_hover:
        state.last_hover = hovering
        state.needs_redraw = True
    if state.needs_redraw:
        redraw(hovering)
        state.needs_redraw = False

docs.title: mlx_do_key_autorepeatoff(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_do_key_autorepeatoff(mlx_ptr)

Turns off keyboard auto-repeat. By default, holding a key generates repeated KeyPress events. After calling this, holding a key fires the event only once until the key is released.

Useful for games where you want to detect a single press, not continuous rapid-fire.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_do_key_autorepeaton(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_do_key_autorepeaton(mlx_ptr)

Turns keyboard auto-repeat back on (default behaviour). Multiple events per second while key is held.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_get_screen_size(mlx_ptr) — returns tuple
docs.text:
ret, screen_width, screen_height = mlx.mlx_get_screen_size(mlx_ptr)

Returns the size of the physical screen (monitor). Can be called before creating any window.

  • Returns: tuple (ret, width, height) in pixels
  • Useful to center a window or make it fullscreen

Center a window on screen:

ret, sw, sh = mlx.mlx_get_screen_size(mlx_ptr)
win_w, win_h = 800, 600
# MLX does not support setting window position, but you know the target offset:
# offset_x = (sw - win_w) // 2
# offset_y = (sh - win_h) // 2

Note: MLX does not provide a function to set the window's position on screen. The OS places it. You can only use the screen size for logic decisions (e.g. choosing tile size to fill the screen).

docs.title: 18. Sync & Flush
docs.text: These functions control when pixel data is actually sent to the screen. Normally you don't need them — mlx_loop handles flushing automatically.

docs.title: mlx_do_sync(mlx_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_do_sync(mlx_ptr)

Flushes all pending drawing commands to the display subsystem. Does not wait for the GPU to finish — just makes sure commands are sent, not cached on the software side.

  • Returns: 0 on success

docs.title: mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, cmd, img_or_win_ptr)
docs.text:
mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_IMAGE_WRITABLE, img_ptr)
mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_WIN_FLUSH, win_ptr)
mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_WIN_COMPLETED, win_ptr)

Fine-grained synchronisation control.

Commands (constants on the Mlx class):

Constant Value Meaning Mlx.SYNC_IMAGE_WRITABLE 1 Wait until image data buffer can be safely written again Mlx.SYNC_WIN_FLUSH 2 Send all pending requests for this window to the server Mlx.SYNC_WIN_COMPLETED 3 Flush AND wait for the server to confirm completion

When to use: - SYNC_IMAGE_WRITABLE: before writing to an image that was just rendered — avoids writing while the GPU is still reading - SYNC_WIN_FLUSH: when you need to force a frame to appear immediately - SYNC_WIN_COMPLETED: when you need to guarantee the frame is fully displayed before continuing

docs.title: 19. Color System
docs.text:
Colors in MLX are unsigned int values. The byte layout depends on the image format reported by mlx_get_data_addr, which can be either:

  • Format 0: B8 G8 R8 A8 (Blue, Green, Red, Alpha)
  • Format 1: A8 R8 G8 B8 (Alpha, Red, Green, Blue)

For mlx_pixel_put and mlx_string_put, use the 0xAARRGGBB notation:

0xFF FF FF FF
  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑
  A  R  G  B

Common colors:

WHITE   = 0xFFFFFFFF
BLACK   = 0xFF000000
RED     = 0xFFFF0000
GREEN   = 0xFF00FF00
BLUE    = 0xFF0000FF
YELLOW  = 0xFFFFFF00
CYAN    = 0xFF00FFFF
MAGENTA = 0xFFFF00FF
GREY    = 0xFF888888

For image pixel buffers (raw bytes):

The 4 bytes are written directly in memory order. On little-endian (all modern PCs): 

# Format 0 (B G R A):
color_bytes = bytes([blue, green, red, alpha])

# Format 1 (A R G B):
color_bytes = bytes([alpha, red, green, blue])

Building a color integer from RGB components:

def rgb(r, g, b, a=255):
    return (a << 24) | (r << 16) | (g << 8) | b

Alpha (transparency): - 255 (0xFF) = fully opaque - 0 = fully transparent - MLX composites images with transparency correctly when rendering

docs.title: A. Hover Effect on a Button
docs.text:
Detect mouse position each frame, switch to a highlight image when hovering:

BTN_X, BTN_Y, BTN_W, BTN_H = 100, 200, 240, 55

def on_loop(param):
    _, mx, my = mlx.mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr)
    hovering = (BTN_X <= mx <= BTN_X + BTN_W and
                BTN_Y <= my <= BTN_Y + BTN_H)

    img = img_btn_hover if hovering else img_btn_normal
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_bg, 0, 0)
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img, BTN_X, BTN_Y)

mlx.mlx_loop_hook(mlx_ptr, on_loop, None)

docs.title: B. Clickable Image Button
docs.text:
def on_mouse(button, x, y, param):
    if button == 1:  # left click
        if BTN_X <= x <= BTN_X + BTN_W and BTN_Y <= y <= BTN_Y + BTN_H:
            do_action()

mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, on_mouse, None)

docs.title: C. Custom Mouse Cursor
docs.text:
Hide the system cursor and draw your own image at the mouse position:

mlx.mlx_mouse_hide(mlx_ptr)

def on_loop(param):
    _, mx, my = mlx.mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr)
    mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_bg, 0, 0)
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_cursor, mx - 8, my - 8)

docs.title: D. Drawing to an Image Buffer (Fast)
docs.text:
img_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_image(mlx_ptr, 800, 600)
data, bpp, sl, fmt = mlx.mlx_get_data_addr(img_ptr)

# Draw a red diagonal line
for i in range(400):
    offset = i * sl + i * 4
    data[offset:offset + 4] = bytes([0x00, 0x00, 0xFF, 0xFF])  # BGRA red

mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img_ptr, 0, 0)

docs.title: E. Multiple Windows
docs.text:
win1 = mlx.mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, 800, 600, "Window 1")
win2 = mlx.mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, 400, 300, "Window 2")

# Each window gets its own hooks
mlx.mlx_key_hook(win1, on_key_win1, None)
mlx.mlx_key_hook(win2, on_key_win2, None)
mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win1, on_mouse_win1, None)
mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win2, on_mouse_win2, None)

# Close just one window
def on_close_win2(param):
    mlx.mlx_destroy_window(mlx_ptr, win2)

mlx.mlx_hook(win2, 33, 0, on_close_win2, None)

docs.title: F. Detecting Key Held Down (KeyPress, not KeyRelease)
docs.text:
# KeyPress fires immediately and repeatedly while held
def on_keypress(key, param):
    if key == 65361:  # left arrow
        state.player_x -= 5
        state.needs_redraw = True

mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, 2, 1, on_keypress, None)  # event 2 = KeyPress

docs.title: G. Scene / State Machine
docs.text:
# Switch between "menu" and "game" without opening a new window
state.scene = "menu"

def on_loop(param):
    if not state.needs_redraw:
        return
    mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
    if state.scene == "menu":
        draw_menu()
    elif state.scene == "game":
        draw_game()
    state.needs_redraw = False

def on_key(key, param):
    if state.scene == "menu" and key == 49:  # '1'
        state.scene = "game"
        state.needs_redraw = True

docs.title: H. Animation / Frame Counter
docs.text:
import time

state.frame = 0

def on_loop(param):
    state.frame += 1
    # Animate every 10 frames
    frame_img = anim_frames[state.frame % len(anim_frames)]
    mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, frame_img, 0, 0)

docs.title: I. Clean Program Exit
docs.text:
def shutdown():
    mlx.mlx_destroy_image(mlx_ptr, img_ptr)
    mlx.mlx_destroy_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)
    mlx.mlx_release(mlx_ptr)

def on_key(key, param):
    if key == 65307:  # ESC
        mlx.mlx_loop_exit(mlx_ptr)

# After mlx_loop returns:
mlx.mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)
shutdown()

docs.title: 21. Limitations & Known Issues
docs.text: Limitation Detail No window positioning Cannot set where on screen the window appears Font is fixed mlx_string_put uses one built-in bitmap font, cannot change size or face PNG loader unreliable Some PNG files fail to load; convert to XPM with ImageMagick for production No Ctrl+C in loop Python cannot catch SIGINT inside mlx_loop. Use Ctrl+\ or os._exit(0) Expose event may not fire On modern composited desktops the expose hook is unreliable; use loop_hook + dirty flag MotionNotify requires button held Event 6 only fires during click-drag; use mlx_mouse_get_pos polling for hover Alpha in mlx_string_put Alpha channel of the color is always forced to 255 (opaque) — you cannot make text semi-transparent mlx_pixel_put is slow Each call is a separate GPU command; use image buffers for bulk drawing No text input There is no text field or input widget; you must build your own using key hooks No built-in UI No buttons, checkboxes, sliders — all must be built using images and hit-testing Image format endian mlx_get_data_addr format can be 0 or 1 — always check before writing pixel bytes

docs.title: 22. Quick Reference Card
docs.text:
INIT
  mlx_ptr = mlx.mlx_init()
  mlx.mlx_release(mlx_ptr)

WINDOW
  win_ptr = mlx.mlx_new_window(mlx_ptr, w, h, "title")
  mlx.mlx_clear_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)       # fill black
  mlx.mlx_destroy_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr)

DRAW DIRECT (slow)
  mlx.mlx_pixel_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, x, y, color)
  mlx.mlx_string_put(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, x, y, color, "text")

IMAGES (fast)
  img = mlx.mlx_new_image(mlx_ptr, w, h)
  data, bpp, sl, fmt = mlx.mlx_get_data_addr(img)
  mlx.mlx_put_image_to_window(mlx_ptr, win_ptr, img, x, y)
  mlx.mlx_destroy_image(mlx_ptr, img)

LOAD FILES
  img, w, h = mlx.mlx_xpm_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, "file.xpm")  # recommended
  img, w, h = mlx.mlx_png_file_to_image(mlx_ptr, "file.png")  # unreliable

LOOP & EVENTS
  mlx.mlx_loop(mlx_ptr)                         # starts loop, never returns
  mlx.mlx_loop_exit(mlx_ptr)                    # exit from inside a hook
  mlx.mlx_key_hook(win_ptr, fn(key,p), param)   # key released
  mlx.mlx_mouse_hook(win_ptr, fn(btn,x,y,p), p) # mouse click
  mlx.mlx_expose_hook(win_ptr, fn(p), param)     # window needs redraw
  mlx.mlx_loop_hook(mlx_ptr, fn(p), param)       # every frame

GENERIC HOOK (all events)
  mlx.mlx_hook(win_ptr, x_event, x_mask, fn, param)
  # x_event: 2=KeyPress  3=KeyRelease  4=BtnPress  5=BtnRelease
  #           6=Motion    7=Enter       8=Leave     33=WindowClose

MOUSE UTILS
  mlx.mlx_mouse_hide(mlx_ptr)
  mlx.mlx_mouse_show(mlx_ptr)
  mlx.mlx_mouse_move(mlx_ptr, x, y)
  ret, x, y = mlx.mlx_mouse_get_pos(mlx_ptr)

KEYBOARD UTILS
  mlx.mlx_do_key_autorepeatoff(mlx_ptr)
  mlx.mlx_do_key_autorepeaton(mlx_ptr)

SCREEN
  ret, w, h = mlx.mlx_get_screen_size(mlx_ptr)

SYNC
  mlx.mlx_do_sync(mlx_ptr)
  mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_IMAGE_WRITABLE, img)
  mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_WIN_FLUSH, win)
  mlx.mlx_sync(mlx_ptr, Mlx.SYNC_WIN_COMPLETED, win)

COLORS  0xAARRGGBB
  WHITE=0xFFFFFFFF  BLACK=0xFF000000  RED=0xFFFF0000
  GREEN=0xFF00FF00  BLUE=0xFF0000FF   YELLOW=0xFFFFFF00

KEY CODES (Linux)
  ESC=65307  Enter=65293  Space=32
  Up=65362   Down=65364   Left=65361  Right=65363
  'a'=97     'z'=122      '0'=48      '1'=49

Documentation written from source: mlx.py, mlx.h, man pages, C source files, and test examples — mlx_CLXV v2.2

docs.title: Makefile
docs.text:
NAME = fly_in.py
PYTHON = python3
VENV = venv
PIP = $(VENV)/bin/python3 -m pip

LEVEL = easy
MAP ?= 01_linear_path.txt

all: install run

# INSTALL VENV
venv:
    @if [ ! -d "$(VENV)" ]; then \
        echo "🛠️  Creating virtual environment..."; \
        $(PYTHON) -m venv $(VENV); \
        echo "✅ Venv created successfully"; \
        echo ""; \
        echo "📌 To activate the virtual environment run:"; \
        echo "source $(VENV)/bin/activate"; \
    else \
        echo "⚠️ Venv already exists"; \
    fi

# INSTALL ALL REQUIREMENTS

install: venv
    @echo "📦 Installing requirements..."
    @$(PIP) install --upgrade pip
    @$(PIP) install -r requirements.txt
    @echo "✅ Installation complete"

# RUN THE GAME
run:
    $(VENV)/bin/python3 $(NAME) assets/maps/$(LEVEL)/$(MAP)

# DEBUGGER
debug:
    @$(VENV)/bin/python3 -m pdb $(NAME) assets/maps/$(LEVEL)/$(MAP)

# CHECK FOR NORM ERRORS
lint:
    @echo "🔍 Running flake8 and mypy..."
    $(VENV)/bin/flake8 .
    $(VENV)/bin/mypy . \
        --warn-return-any \
        --warn-unused-ignores \
        --ignore-missing-imports \
        --disallow-untyped-defs \
        --check-untyped-defs
    @echo "✅ Lint completed"

lint-strict:
    @echo "🧠 Running strict checks..."
    $(VENV)/bin/flake8 .
    $(VENV)/bin/mypy . \
        --strict
    @echo "✅ Strict lint completed"

# CLEANERS
clean:
    @echo "🧹 Cleaning cache files..."
    find . -name "__pycache__" -exec rm -rf {} +
    find . -name "*.pyc" -delete
    rm -rf .mypy_cache
    @echo "✅ Partial clean complete"

fclean: clean
    @echo "💣 Removing virtual environment..."
    rm -rf $(VENV)
    @echo "✅ Full clean complete"

re: fclean install

.PHONY: all venv install run debug lint clean fclean re

docs.text:
Beginner-friendly documentation about Makefiles for Python projects, automation workflows, linting, virtual environments, and common development commands.

📎 A complete example Makefile is provided alongside this guide for reference and practical implementation examples.

docs.title: 📖 What is a Makefile?
docs.text:
A Makefile is a file used to automate terminal commands.

Instead of typing long commands repeatedly, you can run:

make

or:

make run

and execute predefined workflows automatically.

docs.title: 🐍 Why Use Makefiles in Python?
docs.text:
Makefiles help: - automate repetitive tasks - standardize project workflows - simplify setup - improve teamwork - reduce mistakes

Very useful for: - 42 projects - game projects - parsers - APIs - collaborative repositories

docs.title: 🛠️ Common Python Makefile Commands
docs.text: ⚙️ Target 📖 Purpose make 🚀 Default workflow make run ▶️ Run project make install 📦 Install dependencies make lint 🔍 Run flake8/mypy make clean 🧹 Remove cache make re ♻️ Rebuild project

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
run:
    python3 main.py

Execute with the command:

make run

docs.title: 🔀 Conditional Statements in Makefiles
docs.text:
Makefiles can also use shell conditionals such as:

@if [ ! -d "$(VENV)" ]; then \
    python3 -m venv $(VENV); \
fi

docs.title: What This Does
docs.text: This checks if the virtual environment folder already exists.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: Part Meaning if Starts the condition [ ! -d "$(VENV)" ] Checks if the directory does NOT exist then Executes the commands below fi Ends the condition

docs.title: Why This is Useful
docs.text:
This prevents: - recreating the virtual environment every time - reinstalling dependencies unnecessarily - accidentally overwriting environments

Very common in Python project setup workflows.

docs.title: Common Example
docs.text:
venv:
    @if [ ! -d "$(VENV)" ]; then \
        python3 -m venv $(VENV); \
    fi

This means: - if venv/ does not exist → create it - otherwise → do nothing

docs.title: 🎯 Targets
docs.text: A target is a command section inside the Makefile.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
install:
    pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 📦 Variables
docs.text:
To Makefiles cleaner and reusable.

Variables are useful to: - reduce repetition - simplify updates - improve readability

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
PYTHON = python3

Used like:

$(PYTHON) main.py

docs.title: 🚀 Default Targets
docs.text: The first target is usually the default target.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
all: run

Running:

make

automatically runs:

make run

docs.title: 🔗 Dependencies
docs.text: Targets can depend on other targets.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
run: install
    python3 main.py

Meaning: - install runs first - then run

docs.title: 🧪 Virtual Environment Example
docs.text:
venv:
    python3 -m venv venv

docs.title: Using the venv Python
docs.text:
run:
    venv/bin/python3 main.py

This guarantees: - correct packages - correct environment

docs.title: 📥 Installing Requirements
docs.text:
install:
    venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 🔍 Linting Example
docs.text:
lint:
    flake8 .
    mypy .

Useful for: - formatting checks - typing checks

docs.title: 🧹 Cleaning Cache Files
docs.text:
clean:
    find . -name "__pycache__" -exec rm -rf {} +

docs.title: 🧨 Full Clean Example
docs.text:
fclean: clean
    rm -rf venv

Removes: - cache files - virtual environment

docs.title: ♻️ Rebuild Example
docs.text:
re: fclean install

clean everything
→ reinstall everything

docs.title: 📌 .PHONY
docs.text: .PHONY prevents Make from confusing targets with real files.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
.PHONY: run clean install

Very common in professional Makefiles.

docs.title: ❌ Using Spaces Instead of Tabs
docs.text:
Wrong:

run:
 python3 main.py

Correct:

run:
    python3 main.py

docs.title: ❌ Missing .PHONY
docs.text: Without .PHONY, Make may behave incorrectly if files share target names.

docs.title: ❌ Using Global Python
docs.text:
Bad:

python3 main.py

Better:

venv/bin/python3 main.py

docs.title: 🧠 Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create virtual environment
  2. Install requirements
  3. Run project
  4. Run linting
  5. Clean cache files when needed

docs.title: 📚 Additional Notes
docs.text: An example Makefile is included alongside this document for reference and practical usage examples.

docs.title: 📚 Final Notes
docs.text:
Understanding Makefiles is an important skill for Python development.

Even simple Makefiles can: - save time - automate repetitive tasks - standardize workflows - improve project organization

docs.title: JSON and Data Validation Guide
docs.text:
A beginner-friendly guide to JSON, serialization, schemas, and data validation in Python.

This document explains: - JSON - serialization - deserialization - validation - schemas - common validation techniques

These concepts are heavily used in: - APIs - web development - configuration files - parsers - databases - game systems - data engineering

docs.title: What is JSON?
docs.text:
JSON stands for:

JavaScript Object Notation

It is a lightweight format used to store and exchange data.

JSON is one of the most common data formats in the world.

docs.title: Why JSON is Popular
docs.text: JSON is: - human readable - easy to parse - language independent - lightweight - widely supported

docs.title: Basic JSON Example
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Sara",
    "age": 20,
    "is_active": true
}

docs.title: JSON Data Types
docs.text: JSON Type Python Equivalent string str number int / float boolean bool object dict array list null None

docs.title: JSON Objects
docs.text: JSON objects are similar to Python dictionaries.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
    "username": "Sara",
    "score": 100
}

Equivalent Python dictionary:

{
    "username": "Sara",
    "score": 100
}

docs.title: JSON Arrays
docs.text: Arrays are similar to Python lists.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
[
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "orange"
]

Equivalent Python list:

["apple", "banana", "orange"]

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: Serialization means converting Python objects into JSON.

docs.title: Why Serialization Matters
docs.text: Serialization is used when: - sending API responses - saving files - storing data - sending network messages

docs.title: Python Serialization Example
docs.text:
import json

data = {
    "name": "Sara",
    "age": 20
}

json_text = json.dumps(data)

print(json_text)

docs.title: json.dumps()
docs.text:
dumps means:

dump string

It converts Python data into a JSON string.

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text: {"name": "Sara", "age": 20}

docs.title: Pretty JSON Formatting
docs.text:
json.dumps(data, indent=4)

Produces readable JSON.

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text: Deserialization means converting JSON into Python objects.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import json

text = '{"name": "Sara", "age": 20}'

data = json.loads(text)

print(data["name"])

docs.title: json.loads()
docs.text:
loads means:

load string

It converts JSON text into Python objects.

docs.title: Writing JSON Files
docs.text:
import json

data = {
    "name": "Sara",
    "score": 42
}

with open("data.json", "w") as file:
    json.dump(data, file, indent=4)

docs.title: Reading JSON Files
docs.text:
import json

with open("data.json", "r") as file:
    data = json.load(file)

print(data)

docs.title: dump vs dumps
docs.text: Function Purpose json.dump Writes JSON to file json.dumps Returns JSON string json.load Reads JSON from file json.loads Reads JSON from string

docs.title: What is Validation?
docs.text:
Validation checks if data is: - correct - complete - safe - expected

Validation prevents: - crashes - invalid data - corrupted systems

docs.title: Example Without Validation
docs.text:
age = int(user_input)

If input is:

hello

the program crashes.

docs.title: Example With Validation
docs.text:
if user_input.isdigit():
    age = int(user_input)
else:
    print("Invalid age")

docs.title: Why Data Validation Matters
docs.text:
Validation is critical in: - APIs - config parsers - user input - databases - file systems

Bad data can: - crash applications - create security problems - corrupt files - break systems

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
A schema defines: - the structure of data - required fields - data types - validation rules

Schemas describe what valid data looks like.

docs.title: Example Schema Concept
docs.text:
User:
- name -> string
- age -> integer
- email -> string

docs.title: Validation Using Pydantic
docs.text: Pydantic validates data using schemas defined as Python classes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int

docs.title: Valid Data
docs.text: User(name="Sara", age=20)

docs.title: Invalid Data
docs.text:
User(name="Sara", age="hello")

This raises:

ValidationError

docs.title: Field Validation
docs.text: Pydantic supports extra validation using Field.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class User(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=99)

docs.title: Validation Rules
docs.text: This means: - age must be >= 18 - age must be <= 99

docs.title: Optional Fields
docs.text:
from typing import Optional

nickname: Optional[str]

Allows: - string - or None

docs.title: Nested Validation
docs.text: Schemas can contain other schemas.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Address(BaseModel):
    city: str


class User(BaseModel):
    address: Address

Pydantic validates nested objects automatically.

docs.title: Custom Validation
docs.text: Sometimes validation depends on multiple fields.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
if duration_days > 365 and crew_size < 5:
    raise ValueError("Crew too small")

docs.title: Common Validation Techniques
docs.text: Validation Type Example Type validation int, str, bool Range validation age >= 18 Length validation min_length=3 Format validation email structure Required fields missing keys Business rules custom logic

docs.title: Invalid Syntax
docs.text:
Bad JSON:

{
    "name": "Sara",
}

Trailing commas are invalid.

docs.title: Wrong Types
docs.text:
{
    "age": "hello"
}

Expected integer: - received string

docs.title: Missing Fields
docs.text:
{
    "name": "Sara"
}

Missing required fields may break validation.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Never trust external JSON blindly.

Always validate: - API data - uploaded files - config files - network messages

docs.title: Config Parser
docs.text:
{
    "width": 20,
    "height": 15
}

docs.title: Game Save Data
docs.text:
{
    "player": "Sara",
    "level": 5,
    "position": [10, 20]
}

docs.title: API Response
docs.text:
{
    "status": "ok",
    "data": {}
}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always validate external data
  • Use schemas for structure
  • Keep JSON readable
  • Use meaningful field names
  • Validate before processing
  • Handle invalid data safely

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Purpose JSON Data exchange format Serialization Python -> JSON Deserialization JSON -> Python Validation Checks correctness Schema Defines data structure Pydantic Validation library

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
JSON and validation are fundamental concepts in modern software development.

Understanding them is essential for: - APIs - game systems - parsers - databases - backend systems - configuration management

Good validation creates: - safer applications - cleaner code - fewer crashes - better debugging - more reliable systems

docs.title: Pydantic v2 - Core Concepts Review
docs.text: This document explains the main Pydantic concepts used in the exercises from the Cosmic Data module (nº9).

docs.title: What is Pydantic?
docs.text:
Pydantic is a Python library used for:

  • Data validation
  • Automatic type conversion
  • Parsing external data
  • Safer and cleaner models

It allows developers to define strict data structures using Python type hints.

docs.title: BaseModel
docs.text:
BaseModel is the foundation of every Pydantic model.

When a class inherits from BaseModel, Pydantic automatically validates the data.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int

docs.title: Creating an object
docs.text: user = User(name="Sara", age=20)

docs.title: Automatic Type Conversion
docs.text: Pydantic automatically converts compatible types.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
user = User(name="Sara", age="20")

Even though "20" is a string, Pydantic converts it into an integer.

docs.title: ValidationError
docs.text: If invalid data is provided, Pydantic raises a ValidationError.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User(name="Sara", age="abc")

Output:

ValidationError

Because "abc" cannot be converted into an integer.

docs.title: Field
docs.text: Field() is used to add validation constraints and metadata to attributes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pydantic import Field

age: int = Field(ge=18, le=80)

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
• ge = greater or equal
  • le = less or equal

This means age must be between 18 and 80.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
name: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=50)

The string: - must contain at least 3 characters - cannot exceed 50 characters

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
power_level: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=100.0)

Useful for percentages and ranges.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text: Pydantic supports default values.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
is_active: bool = True

If no value is provided, the field automatically becomes True.

docs.title: Optional Fields
docs.text: Optional fields may contain a value or None.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from typing import Optional

notes: Optional[str]

Equivalent to:

str | None

docs.title: Enum
docs.text: Enums restrict a field to predefined values.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from enum import Enum

class Rank(str, Enum):
    CAPTAIN = "captain"
    COMMANDER = "commander"

docs.title: Why use Enum?
docs.text: Enums prevent invalid values.

docs.title: Valid
docs.text: rank="captain"

docs.title: Invalid
docs.text:
rank="banana"

This would raise a validation error.

docs.title: model_validator
docs.text:
@model_validator is used for custom validation logic.

It is useful when validation depends on multiple fields.

docs.title: Pydantic v2 Syntax
docs.text:
from pydantic import model_validator

@model_validator(mode='after')

docs.title: mode='after'
docs.text:
This means:

  1. Pydantic validates all fields first
  2. Then your custom validation logic runs

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
@model_validator(mode='after')
def validate_contact(self):

    if self.contact_type == "physical" and not self.is_verified:
        raise ValueError("Physical contacts must be verified")

    return self

This type of validation cannot be done with Field() alone.

docs.title: return self
docs.text:
Inside a model validator, return self is required.

It returns the validated model instance.

docs.title: Nested Models
docs.text: Nested models are models inside other models.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class CrewMember(BaseModel):
    name: str

class SpaceMission(BaseModel):
    crew: list[CrewMember]

docs.title: What happens automatically?
docs.text: Pydantic: - validates the list - validates every CrewMember - converts data automatically

docs.title: Dictionary Unpacking (**data)
docs.text: **data converts a dictionary into keyword arguments.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
data = {
    "name": "Sara",
    "age": 20
}

User(**data)

Equivalent to:

User(name="Sara", age=20)

docs.title: Datetime Validation
docs.text: Pydantic automatically parses datetime values.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime

created_at: datetime

It can convert: - datetime objects - valid datetime strings - timestamps

docs.title: Field
docs.text: Used for single-field validation.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
age: int = Field(ge=18)

Validates only the age field.

docs.title: model_validator
docs.text: Used for validation involving multiple fields.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
if duration_days > 365 and crew_size < 5:
    raise ValueError("Long missions require larger crews")

This depends on multiple attributes.

docs.title: Main Advantages of Pydantic
docs.text:
• Cleaner code
  • Automatic validation
  • Better error messages
  • Automatic type conversion
  • Easier API and data handling
  • Strong typing support

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Purpose BaseModel Creates validated models Field Adds constraints to fields Enum Restricts possible values ValidationError Raised when validation fails model_validator Custom validation logic Optional Allows None values Nested Models Models inside other models datetime Automatic datetime parsing

docs.title: ✨ Python Dunder Methods Guide
docs.text: Beginner-friendly documentation about Python dunder methods (magic methods), special object behavior, and common object-oriented patterns.

docs.title: 📚 Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 📖 What are Dunder Methods?
  • 🚀 init
  • 🖨️ str
  • 🔍 repr
  • 📏 len
  • ⚖️ eq
  • ➕ add
  • 📦 getitem
  • 🔄 iter
  • 🎮 Real 42 Examples
  • ⚠️ Common Beginner Mistakes
  • 📚 Best Practices
  • 📚 Final Notes

docs.title: 📖 What are Dunder Methods?
docs.text:
Dunder methods are: - special Python methods - surrounded by double underscores

Example:

__init__

The word: 

dunder

means: 

double underscore

docs.title: Why Dunder Methods Exist
docs.text: They allow Python objects to: - behave like built-in types - customize operators - customize printing - customize comparisons - support iteration

docs.title: 🚀 init
docs.text:
__init__ runs automatically when an object is created.

Used for: - initializing attributes - preparing object state

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Player:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

docs.title: Creating the Object
docs.text: player = Player("Sara")

docs.title: 🖨️ str
docs.text: __str__ controls: - readable object printing

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Player:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Player({self.name})"

docs.title: Using str
docs.text:
player = Player("Sara")

print(player)

Output:

Player(Sara)

docs.title: Why str is Useful
docs.text:
Without __str__, Python prints:

<object at 0x123456>

which is not very readable.

docs.title: 🔍 repr
docs.text: __repr__ provides: - developer/debug representation

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Enemy:

    def __repr__(self):
        return "Enemy()"

docs.title: Difference Between str and repr
docs.text: Method Purpose __str__ User-friendly output __repr__ Developer/debug output

docs.title: 📏 len
docs.text: __len__ controls: - object length behavior

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Inventory:

    def __init__(self):
        self.items = ["Sword", "Potion"]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

docs.title: Using len()
docs.text:
inventory = Inventory()

print(len(inventory))

Output:

2

docs.title: ⚖️ eq
docs.text: __eq__ controls: - equality comparison

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Player:

    def __init__(self, score):
        self.score = score

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.score == other.score

docs.title: Using Equality
docs.text:
player1 = Player(10)
player2 = Player(10)

print(player1 == player2)

Output:

True

docs.title: ➕ add
docs.text: __add__ customizes: - the + operator

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Coins:

    def __init__(self, amount):
        self.amount = amount

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Coins(self.amount + other.amount)

docs.title: Using +
docs.text:
c1 = Coins(5)
c2 = Coins(10)

result = c1 + c2

docs.title: 📦 getitem
docs.text: __getitem__ allows: - indexing with []

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Inventory:

    def __init__(self):
        self.items = ["Sword", "Potion"]

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self.items[index]

docs.title: Using Indexing
docs.text:
inventory = Inventory()

print(inventory[0])

Output:

Sword

docs.title: 🔄 iter
docs.text: __iter__ allows: - iteration with loops

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Inventory:

    def __init__(self):
        self.items = ["Sword", "Potion"]

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.items)

docs.title: Using Iteration
docs.text:
for item in inventory:
    print(item)

docs.title: Maze String Representation
docs.text:
def __str__(self):

Useful for: - ASCII maze printing

docs.title: Position Comparison
docs.text:
def __eq__(self, other):

Useful for: - coordinate comparison - pathfinding

docs.title: Inventory Length
docs.text:
def __len__(self):

Useful for: - item systems

docs.title: Custom Containers
docs.text:
def __getitem__(self, index):

Useful for: - grid systems - tile access

docs.title: ❌ Returning Wrong Types
docs.text:
Bad:

def __len__(self):
    return "five"

__len__ must return: - integer

docs.title: ❌ Forgetting other in eq
docs.text:
Wrong:

def __eq__(self):

Correct:

def __eq__(self, other):

docs.title: ❌ Overcomplicating Dunder Methods
docs.text: Keep behavior: - simple - predictable - readable

docs.title: ❌ Forgetting Return Values
docs.text:
Example:

def __str__(self):
    print("Player")

Wrong because: - __str__ must RETURN a string

docs.title: 📚 Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep dunder methods simple
  • Return correct types
  • Use dunder methods only when useful
  • Avoid unnecessary operator overloads
  • Focus on readability

docs.title: 🧠 Why Dunder Methods Matter
docs.text:
Dunder methods help objects: - behave naturally - integrate with Python syntax - support built-in operations - feel more flexible

They are heavily used in: - frameworks - libraries - games - APIs - custom containers

docs.title: 📚 Final Notes
docs.text:
Dunder methods are one of the most powerful features of Python OOP.

Understanding them helps create: - cleaner APIs - more intuitive objects - reusable systems - better project architecture

They become increasingly useful in larger and more advanced Python projects.

docs.title: 🧠 Python Introspection & Useful Dunder Methods Guide
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly documentation about useful Python dunder attributes and introspection tools commonly used for debugging, classes, logging, and development workflows.

This document explains: - __name__ - __class__ - __dict__ - __module__ - type() - getting class names - getting function names - debugging patterns - introspection basics

docs.title: 📚 Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 📖 What is Introspection?
  • 🏷️ name
  • 🏛️ class
  • 📦 dict
  • 📁 module
  • 🔍 type()

  • ⚙️ Getting Function Names

  • 🎮 Real 42 Examples
  • ⚠️ Common Beginner Mistakes
  • 📚 Best Practices
  • 📚 Final Notes

docs.title: 📖 What is Introspection?
docs.text:
Introspection means: - inspecting Python objects dynamically

Python allows you to inspect: - classes - objects - functions - modules - attributes

Very useful for: - debugging - logging - parsers - large projects

docs.title: 🏷️ name
docs.text: __name__ stores: - the name of a function - the name of a module

docs.title: Function Example
docs.text:
def move():
    pass

print(move.__name__)

Output:

move

docs.title: Module Example
docs.text:
print(__name__)

Usually outputs:

__main__

when running the file directly.

docs.title: 🏛️ class
docs.text: __class__ gives: - the object's class

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Drone:
    pass

drone = Drone()

print(drone.__class__)

Output:

<class '__main__.Drone'>

docs.title: 📦 dict
docs.text: __dict__ stores: - object attributes

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Player:

    def __init__(self):
        self.hp = 100
        self.name = "Sara"

player = Player()

print(player.__dict__)

docs.title: Output
docs.text: {'hp': 100, 'name': 'Sara'}

docs.title: Why dict is Useful
docs.text: Useful for: - debugging - serialization - quick inspection

docs.title: 📁 module
docs.text: __module__ shows: - where the class/function was defined

docs.title: Example
docs.text: print(Player.__module__)

docs.title: 🔍 type()
docs.text: type() returns: - the object's type

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
print(type(player))

Output:

<class '__main__.Player'>

docs.title: 🎯 Getting Class Names
docs.text: Very common debugging pattern.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
print(player.__class__.__name__)

Output:

Player

docs.title: Why This is Useful
docs.text: Useful for: - debugging - logging - error reporting - game systems

docs.title: ⚙️ Getting Function Names
docs.text: Functions also store their names.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
def validate():
    pass

print(validate.__name__)

Output:

validate

docs.title: Using Inside Debugging
docs.text: print(f"Failed inside function: {validate.__name__}")

docs.title: Printing Class Names
docs.text: print(type(obj).__name__)

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text: Maze

docs.title: Printing Function Names
docs.text: print(function.__name__)

docs.title: Printing Object Attributes
docs.text: print(obj.__dict__)

docs.title: Printing Exception Types
docs.text: print(type(e).__name__)

docs.title: Parser Debugging
docs.text: print(type(zone).__name__)

docs.title: Maze Debugging
docs.text: print(maze.__dict__)

docs.title: Function Tracking
docs.text: print(generate_maze.__name__)

docs.title: Error Reporting
docs.text: print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")

docs.title: ❌ Confusing name Types
docs.text:
Functions: - have __name__

Objects: - usually do not

docs.title: ❌ Printing Entire Objects Accidentally
docs.text:
print(obj)

may not be useful without: - __str__

docs.title: ❌ Modifying dict Incorrectly
docs.text: Changing __dict__ directly may: - create bugs - break objects

docs.title: 📚 Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use introspection mainly for debugging
  • Keep debug prints readable
  • Use meaningful class names
  • Avoid excessive debug output
  • Prefer structured logging in large projects

docs.title: 🧠 Why Introspection Matters
docs.text:
Introspection helps: - understand objects dynamically - debug faster - inspect large systems - improve logging

Very useful in: - parsers - frameworks - MLX projects - game systems - debugging tools

docs.title: 📚 Final Notes
docs.text:
Python introspection is one of the language's most powerful features.

Understanding these tools helps: - debug efficiently - inspect objects dynamically - improve architecture - build better development workflows

These patterns become increasingly useful in larger Python projects.

docs.title: 📦 Python Packages Guide
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly documentation about Python packages, imports, modules, and project organization.

This document explains: - what packages are - how imports work - __init__.py - package organization - absolute vs relative imports - common beginner mistakes - project structure examples

docs.title: 📚 Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 📖 What is a Package?
  • 📦 What is a Module?
  • 🧱 Basic Package Structure
  • 📥 Importing Modules
  • 📌 init.py
  • 🌿 Absolute Imports
  • 🔗 Relative Imports
  • 🛠️ Organizing Large Projects
  • 📌 init.py Contents
  • ⚠️ Common Beginner Mistakes
  • 📚 Final Notes

docs.title: 📖 What is a Package?
docs.text:
A package is a folder containing Python modules.

Packages help: - organize code - separate logic - structure large projects - improve readability

docs.title: 📦 What is a Module?
docs.text:
A module is simply:

a Python file

Example:

utils.py

This file itself is a module.

docs.title: 🧱 Basic Package Structure
docs.text:
project/
│
├── main.py
├── parser/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── config_parser.py
│   └── validator.py
│
└── render/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── draw.py

docs.title: Import Entire Module
docs.text:
import math

Usage:

math.sqrt(25)

docs.title: Import Specific Function
docs.text:
from math import sqrt

Usage:

sqrt(25)

docs.title: 📌 init.py
docs.text:
__init__.py tells Python that a folder should behave like a package.

Without it, imports may fail in some project structures.

docs.title: 🌿 Absolute Imports
docs.text: Absolute imports start from the project root.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: from parser.config_parser import parse_config

docs.title: 🔗 Relative Imports
docs.text: Relative imports use dots (.).

docs.title: Example
docs.text: from .validator import validate_config

docs.title: 🛠️ Organizing Large Projects
docs.text:
Example organization:

project/
│
├── core/
├── parsing/
├── render/
├── utils/
├── tests/
└── assets/
└── main.py

And each folder would have a init.py file to make it a package.

docs.title: 📌 init.py Contents
docs.text:
In many Python projects, __init__.py is often left empty.

Example:

# __init__.py

This is completely normal and commonly used only to mark the folder as a package.

docs.title: Why Leave It Empty?
docs.text: An empty __init__.py: - keeps the package simple - avoids unnecessary imports - helps Python recognize the directory as a package

docs.title: What Can Be Inside init.py?
docs.text: Although often empty, it may also contain: - package imports - helper variables - package initialization code - exposed public functions/classes

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from .config_parser import parse_config
from .validator import validate_config

This allows imports like:

from parser import parse_config

instead of:

from parser.config_parser import parse_config

docs.title: Why This is Useful
docs.text:
This can: - simplify imports - expose public APIs - improve package organization

Very common in: - libraries - frameworks - large Python projects

docs.title: Good Practice
docs.text:
For beginner projects: - keeping __init__.py empty is completely fine

As projects grow larger: - it may be used to organize package exports and initialization logic

docs.title: ❌ Missing init.py
docs.text:
Problem:

ModuleNotFoundError

docs.title: ❌ Circular Imports
docs.text:
Example:

# a.py imports b.py
# b.py imports a.py

docs.title: ❌ Running Files Directly
docs.text:
Bad:

python3 parser/config_parser.py

Better:

python3 main.py

docs.title: 📚 Final Notes
docs.text:
Understanding packages is extremely important for modern Python development.

Good package organization helps: - readability - maintainability - debugging - scalability - teamwork

docs.title: Python Virtual Environments Guide
docs.text:
A beginner-friendly guide to Python virtual environments and package management.

This document explains: - venv - activation - pip - requirements.txt - Poetry - PEP 668 - common problems in 42 School environments

Virtual environments are essential for modern Python development.

docs.title: What is a Virtual Environment?
docs.text:
A virtual environment is an isolated Python environment.

It allows each project to: - have its own packages - use different library versions - avoid conflicts with system Python

Without virtual environments: - projects may break each other - package versions may conflict - system Python can become unstable

docs.title: Why Use Virtual Environments?
docs.text: Virtual environments help: - isolate dependencies - create reproducible projects - avoid permission issues - protect system Python - simplify collaboration

docs.title: Creating a Virtual Environment
docs.text: Python includes venv by default.

docs.title: Create venv
docs.text:
python3 -m venv venv

This creates a folder called:

venv/

Containing: - Python executable - pip - installed packages - activation scripts

docs.title: Common Naming
docs.text:
Most projects use:

venv/

Other common names: - .venv - env

docs.title: Activating the Virtual Environment
docs.text: The environment must be activated before installing packages.

docs.title: Linux / macOS
docs.text: source venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Windows CMD
docs.text: venv\Scripts\activate.bat

docs.title: Windows PowerShell
docs.text: venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

docs.title: Successful Activation
docs.text:
The terminal usually changes.

Example:

(venv) user@computer:~/project$

This means the environment is active.

docs.title: Checking the Python Path
docs.text:
Use:

which python3

Example output:

/home/user/project/venv/bin/python3

If it shows:

/usr/bin/python3

then the venv is probably NOT activated.

docs.title: Deactivating the Environment
docs.text:
deactivate

This returns to the system Python.

docs.title: pip
docs.text:
pip is Python's package manager.

Used for: - installing packages - updating packages - removing packages

docs.title: Installing Packages
docs.text: pip install pydantic

docs.title: Installing Specific Versions
docs.text: pip install "pydantic>=2"

docs.title: Installing Multiple Packages
docs.text: pip install flake8 mypy requests

docs.title: Viewing Installed Packages
docs.text: pip list

docs.title: requirements.txt
docs.text:
requirements.txt stores project dependencies.

Useful for: - reproducibility - collaboration - deployment

docs.title: Creating requirements.txt
docs.text: pip freeze > requirements.txt

docs.title: Example requirements.txt
docs.text:
pydantic==2.11.0
mypy==1.15.0
flake8==7.2.0

docs.title: Installing from requirements.txt
docs.text: pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Why requirements.txt Matters
docs.text: Without it: - other users may install wrong versions - projects may stop working - environments become inconsistent

docs.title: Poetry
docs.text:
Poetry is a more advanced Python dependency manager.

It replaces: - pip - requirements.txt - manual dependency handling

docs.title: Poetry Features
docs.text: Poetry: - manages dependencies - creates virtual environments - handles package versions - simplifies project management

docs.title: Installing Poetry
docs.text:
Linux/macOS:

curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -

docs.title: Creating a Poetry Project
docs.text: poetry init

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text: poetry add pydantic

docs.title: Activating Poetry Environment
docs.text: poetry shell

docs.title: Installing from pyproject.toml
docs.text: poetry install

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text:
Poetry stores dependencies in:

pyproject.toml

Instead of: - requirements.txt

docs.title: Example pyproject.toml
docs.text:
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = "^3.10"
pydantic = "^2.11"

docs.title: PEP 668
docs.text:
PEP 668 protects system Python environments.

Modern Linux distributions may block:

pip install package

outside virtual environments.

docs.title: Common Error
docs.text:
externally-managed-environment

This is extremely common on: - Ubuntu - Debian - 42 machines

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text: The operating system wants to protect: - system Python - system packages - package manager integrity

docs.title: Recommended Solution
docs.text:
Use virtual environments:

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

Then install packages normally.

docs.title: Alternative Solution
docs.text:
Sometimes users install locally:

pip install --user package

But virtual environments are cleaner.

docs.title: Common Problems in 42 School
docs.text: 42 environments often have: - limited permissions - restricted system access - outdated packages - disk quota issues

docs.title: Common Problem: No Permission
docs.text:
Example:

Permission denied

Usually solved by: - using venv - avoiding sudo

docs.title: Common Problem: PEP 668
docs.text:
Example:

externally-managed-environment

Solution: - create a venv

docs.title: Common Problem: No Space Left on Device
docs.text:
Example:

OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device

Very common in: - /tmp - home directories - cached pip files

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
Clean pip cache:

pip cache purge

Remove unused venvs:

rm -rf venv

docs.title: Common Problem: Wrong Python Version
docs.text:
Check version:

python3 --version

docs.title: Common Problem: Missing Packages
docs.text:
Example:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pydantic'

Usually means: - venv not activated - package not installed

docs.title: Common Problem: which python3
docs.text:
If this returns:

/usr/bin/python3

the venv is probably inactive.

docs.title: Common Problem: Broken venv
docs.text:
Sometimes virtual environments break.

Fix:

rm -rf venv
python3 -m venv venv

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Create project folder:

mkdir my_project
cd my_project

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Create virtual environment:

python3 -m venv venv

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Activate environment:

source venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Install dependencies:

pip install pydantic mypy flake8

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text:
Save dependencies:

pip freeze > requirements.txt

docs.title: Recommended .gitignore
docs.text:
Do NOT upload virtual environments to GitHub.

Example:

venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always use virtual environments
  • Never commit venv folders
  • Keep requirements.txt updated
  • Prefer precise package versions
  • Activate venv before working
  • Avoid using sudo pip install

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Tool / Concept Purpose venv Isolated Python environment pip Package manager requirements.txt Stores dependencies Poetry Advanced dependency manager PEP 668 Protects system Python activate Enables virtual environment

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Virtual environments are one of the most important parts of modern Python development.

Understanding them helps avoid: - dependency conflicts - broken projects - permission issues - package problems

This becomes especially important in: - 42 projects - team environments - APIs - large Python applications - deployment systems

docs.text:
Beginner-friendly documentation about Python exceptions, error handling, try/except blocks, and debugging practices.

This document explains: - exceptions - errors - try - except - finally - else - custom exceptions - common debugging patterns

docs.text:

  • 🧹 finally
